units.tr: The third mark of the true and visible Church on earth is a long-lasting duration, never interrupted, according to the mind and belief of Bellarmine, which he expressed in lib. 4. de notis eccl. c. 6. To this may be referred what Socolovius argues concerning the perpetual preservation of the true divine worship, lib. 2. c. 6. Likewise, Mühlhusius's disputation on the perseverance of Roman doctrine from the beginning down to the present belongs here, disp. de fide seu religione, thes. 4. How far all of this is from the truth we shall, by the grace of God, now examine.

(1) Is a long-lasting duration, never interrupted, a mark of the Church? (2) Is constancy a sign of true doctrine? (3) Is the Roman doctrine alone, as it now is, constant? (4) Does the filth of Papism stand out among the most ancient heresies? (5) Was the reformed doctrine alone in existence sixteen hundred years ago? units.la: Conclusio prima est. Duratio diu-turna nec unquam interrupta non est nota eccle-sia. Quando durationem dico, exsistentiæ continuationem ac perseverationem intelligo. Pernotam, ut moris est in hac disputatione, denoto signum certum minimeq; fallax, quo rei natura ostenditur. Ecclesia capitur pro externo ac visibili cœtu Deum secundum verbum suum rite colentium. Assertionis fundamentum est, quod duratio est communissimum π[?]άθος & affectio omnium omnino entium. Quicquid enim exsistit, durationem habet vel momentaneam, vel temporariam, vel æternam. Quod vero diutinam perpetuataq; duratione spectat, ea quoq; inter ecclesiæ fines haud quaquam coercita, inter plura dispescitur. Etenim regnum Satanæ æmulum ecclesiæ Christi nullo temporis spatio intercalatum pariter durat, & durabit in sæculum, etiam in mediis inferorum flammis post sæculi finem, sine ullo fine. Quid ergo? Dicemus adhuc ecclesiæ Christi insigne ac privilegium, quo præ aliis gaudeat & eminet, esse durationem? Ita quidem Bellarmino visum visam est, sed quàm verè ac rectè, jam videa- mus. Is, tertia, inquit, nota est duratio diuturna, nec unquam interrupta. Ecclesia enim dicitur catholica, non solum quia semper fuit, sed etiam quia semper erit. Hinc exstrui- tur talis argumentatio. Quae ecclesia dicitur catholica, ejus nota est diuturna duratio. Quis non videat & rideat majoris infirmitatem? An ex aliis nullis causis ecclesia dici meretur catholica, quàm ob durationem? Catholica est, quòd non ex Judaeorum gente modò, sed ex omnibus populis colligitur; quòd non particulam ex scripturis decerpit, sed universas amplectitur, quòd non privatis & propriis opinionibus occupatur, sed publicam & communissimam Spiritus S. in scriptura loquentis mentem sequitur. Has illa potiores causas credimus, de quibus ecclesia catholici nominis gloria insignis est. Nam illa de causa regnum satanae ne latum quidem culmum verae ecclesiae cederet. Durabit n. & illud usque ad finem mundi, uti supra diximus; quoniam semper erunt palea cum tritico usque ad ventilationem; semper erunt zizania usque ad messem, quae est συντέλεια τῆς αἰῶνος [?], i. e. consummatio mundi, Matth. 13. 39. Interim Bellarm. sententiae suae stabilimentum petit ex Dan. 9. Regnum quod in aeternum non dissipabitur. Sed locus ille legitur ap. Dan. e. 2. v. 44. Suscitabit Deus cœli regnū, quod in secula non destruetur. Item ita ut incuria operarū 6. cum 9. permutari potuerit, si ad hunc locum adversarius respexerit. Sed quorsum hoc? an ut ostendatur durationem esse notam ecclesiæ? At non dicitur sola ecclesia durare in secula. An ut probetur, Romanam ecclesiam in secula duraturam? At nullo verbulo illa attingitur: aut cœlum pariter cum inferis miscetur. Aliud n. est regnum cœliac Christi, aliud regnum papæ & antichristi. Adde, quòd nihil juvet papistas speciosus catholicorum titulus, quoniam eum sibi per vim rapiunt, non a jure accipiunt; quomodo ipse Bellarminus omnem se hæreticorum mantelo palliare fatetur. Deinde adducit illud Act. 5 v. 38. & 39. Si est ex hominibus consilium hoc, sive opus iste, dissolvetur: sin ex Deo est, non poterit illud dissolvere. Quis logicorum ex hoc dicto demonstraverit durationem esse notam ecclesiæ? Gamaliel populi furentes animos componituros docet, opus Dei ab homine nemine solvi posse: proindeque cavendum esse, ne quid temere aut malitiose adversus Deum agatur. Tertio idem vult conficere ex 2 Tim. 3. v. 9. sed ultra non proficient, ait apostolus de hæreticis. Hinc vero concludes, hæreticos non durare! ecclesiam durare solam! Ineptè. Non enim de duratione hæreseon id accipiendum, sed de hæreticohæreticorum persequutione, quâ turbant ecclesiam. Ait enim apostolus, extremis diebus instare tempora molesta, v. 1. Et ratio, quare non perpetim æquè molesti esse queant, indicatur, quoniam amentia illorum evidenserit omnibus, v. 9. De duratione autem agitur v. 15. Improbi a. homines & impostores procedent in peius, tum seducentes, tum seducti. Quarto Cyprianum citat, qui l. 4. ep. 2. dicit schismaticos semper inter initia fervere, incrementa vero habere non posse, sed statim cum prava sua accumulatione deficere. Atqui hinc non est concludere, duratione esse notam ecclesiæ. Nam defectio schismaticorum subitaria non est universe vera. Multi n. diu in schismate, errore, hæresi durant. Damnato exemplo sunt Ariani, Muhamedani, alii. Ut autem quædam hæreses quasi in herba oppressæ intereunt, ita & quædam subnascentes veræ ecclesiæ a verbi & cultus divini puritate aut saltem a zelo remittunt. Ephesina ecclesia extra dubium fuit vera ecclesia. Ejus tamen angelo dicit Dominus: Habeo aliquid adversum te, quod charitatem tuam primam omiseris. Memor esto itaque unde excideris, resipisce et priora opera facito, Apocal. 2 v. 4 f. Imo ubi nunc sunt florentissimæ illæ orientis ecclesiæ omnes? Deletæ sunt, non cadaverosæ, sed cadavera mera. Non igitur quicquam agitur, ad probandam tertiam hanc notam, auctoritate Cypriani, à quo Augustinus non sentit diversum, quando nonnullas hæreses aquarum more decurrere ac siccari tradit, Psal. 57: Itaeminat: Multa hæreses jam emortua sunt, cu-currerunt in rivis, quantum potuerunt, de-currerunt, siccati sunt rivi, vix eorum memoria reperitur, vel quia fuerint. Multæ, inquit, non omnes. Similiter quis dixerit, multas ex veris ecclesiis emortuas, quò nervus adversarii rumperetur. Atq; hoc dixisse satis est.
units.tr: The first conclusion is this. Long-lasting duration, never interrupted, is not a mark of the Church. When I speak of duration, I understand the continuation and perseverance of existence. By a mark, as is customary in this disputation, I mean a certain and least fallible sign by which the nature of a thing is shown. The Church is taken for the external and visible assembly of those who worship God rightly according to his Word. The foundation of the assertion is that duration is the most common affection and attribute of all beings. For whatever exists has duration, either momentary, temporary, or eternal. Now what looks to long and perpetual duration is not at all confined within the limits of the Church, but is shared among many things. For the kingdom of Satan, the rival of the Church of Christ, likewise endures through no interval of time, and will endure forever, even in the midst of the flames of hell after the end of the age, without any end. What then? Shall we still say that duration is the distinguishing mark and privilege of the Church of Christ, by which it rejoices and stands out above others? Indeed this seemed so to Bellarmine, but let us see how truly and rightly. He says: The third mark is long-lasting duration, never interrupted. For the Church is called catholic not only because it has always existed, but also because it will always exist. From this the following argument is built. The Church that is called catholic has long-lasting duration as its mark. Who would not see and laugh at the weakness of the greater premise? Or is the Church deserving of the name catholic for no other causes than duration? It is catholic because it is gathered not only from the nation of the Jews but from all peoples; because it does not pick out a fragment from the Scriptures but embraces them all; because it is not occupied with private and personal opinions but follows the public and most common mind of the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture. These are the more important causes we believe, by which the Church is distinguished by the glory of the catholic name. For the kingdom of Satan would not yield even a small stalk to the true Church for that reason. For it too will endure until the end of the world, as we said above; since there will always be chaff with the wheat until the winnowing; there will always be tares until the harvest, which is συντέλεια τῆς αἰῶνος [?], i.e. the consummation of the age, Matt. 13:39. Meanwhile Bellarmine seeks the support of his opinion from Dan. 9: A kingdom which shall never be destroyed. But that passage is read in Dan. 2:44: God will raise up a kingdom of heaven, which shall never be destroyed. Likewise, by the carelessness of copyists the 6 could have been swapped for the 9, if the opponent had looked to this passage. But to what end is this? To show that duration is a mark of the Church? But the Church alone is not said to endure forever. Or to prove that the Roman Church will endure forever? But it is touched on by no word of it; nor is heaven mixed together with hell in the same way. For the kingdom of Christ in heaven is one thing, the kingdom of the pope and Antichrist another. Add that the splendid title of the Catholics helps the Papists nothing, since they seize it for themselves by force and do not receive it by right; as Bellarmine himself confesses that he covers himself with the cloak of heretics. Next he brings forward Acts 5:38-39: If this counsel or work is of men, it will be dissolved; but if it is of God, it cannot dissolve it. Which logician would prove from this saying that duration is a mark of the Church? Gamaliel teaches that raging peoples will calm their minds, and that the work of God can be dissolved by no man; and therefore that care must be taken not to do anything rashly or maliciously against God. Thirdly he wishes to draw the same conclusion from 2 Tim. 3:9: But they shall proceed no further, says the apostle of heretics. From this, however, you would conclude that heretics do not endure and that the Church alone endures! Absurdly. For this must not be understood of the duration of heresies, but of the persecution of the heretics, by which they disturb the Church. For the apostle says: In the last days grievous times shall come, v. 1. And the reason why they cannot always be equally troublesome is indicated: because their madness will be evident to all, v. 9. But duration is treated of in v. 13: But evil men and impostors shall wax worse and worse, deceiving and being deceived. Fourthly he cites Cyprian, who in book 4, letter 2, says that schismatics always glow at the beginning, but can never have growth, and immediately fail with their own wicked accumulation. Yet it does not follow from this that duration is a mark of the Church. For the sudden failure of schismatics is not universally true. Many persist long in schism, error, and heresy. Arians and Muhammadans, and others, are examples that have been condemned. And just as some heresies perish, crushed as if in the blade, so also some true churches, springing up, decline from the purity of the Word and the worship of God, or at least from zeal. The church at Ephesus was beyond doubt a true church. Yet the Lord says to its angel: I have something against you, because you have left your first love. Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works, Rev. 2:4f. Indeed, where now are all those most flourishing churches of the East? They have been destroyed, not as corpses, but as mere corpses. Nothing is therefore accomplished, for proving this third mark, by the authority of Cyprian, from whom Augustine does not differ when he hands down that some heresies run down like waters and dry up, Ps. 57: he says thus: Many heresies have already died; they have run in streams as far as they could, they have run down, the streams have dried up, and scarcely any memory of them is found, or whether they ever existed. Many, he says, not all. Similarly, someone might say that many true churches have died, so that the adversary's sinew would be broken. And it is enough to have said this.

units.la: Conclusio secunda est. Constantia non [?] est vera doctrinæ indicium. Hoc contra Mühl-hufinum, ne forte erres, dextrè ac discretim est accipiendum. Constantia enim alia est moralis, sive virtus sive virtutis communis affectio, de quâ hîc nihil dicere attinet: alia metaphysica, atq; idem est quod duratio, quâ ens sibi constat, seu permanet. Indicium quoq; aliud est proprium ac certum, quod rem indubitato indicat: aliud commune atq; incertum, quod rem probabiliter declarat. Moralis quidem constantia veram doctrinam à virtute alienam non esse communiter indicat: metaphysica verò ei entis communem affectionem tribuit: neutra autem est proprium ejus signum sive indicium, quo à falsis dogmatibus certissimè discernatur. Verisimile ergo dicamus veritatis indicium, juxta illud vetus: μόνιμον ἀληθείας κριτήριον[?]. Non tamen imus infitias, veram & salutarem doctrinam esse constantissimam, imo aeternam, uti ex sacris literis liquidum est, Psal. 119. Matth. 5. Marc. 13. Luc. 15[?]. 1. Pet. 1. 23. 25. Atq; id tantum evincit comparatio, quam Mülhusi-nus hisce verbis instituit: Ut necesse est ecclesiam veram Christi constantem esse, & eandem perseverantem, quum sit supra firmam petram fundatam; ita etiam veram doctrinam & catholicam, non solum antiquam (nam sunt etiam multae antiquissimae haereses) sed etiam unam eandemq; constantem esse, perseveratemq; necesse est. Recte illa quidem dicuntur, at ni-hil tamen faciunt ad ostendendum, constan-tiam esse verae doctrinae proprium atq; indu-bitatum indicium, quale omnino ab eo exi-gitur, quin in tanta religionum inter Christia-nos varie-tate, unam prudenter ac tuto eligere voluerit.
units.tr: The second conclusion is this. Constancy is not a sign of true doctrine. This, against Mühlhusius, lest perhaps you err, must be taken carefully and with distinction. For constancy is of one kind, moral, whether a virtue or a common affection of virtue, about which it is not needful to say anything here; another kind is metaphysical, and this is the same as duration, by which a being remains consistent with itself, or persists. A sign too is of one kind proper and certain, which indicates a thing beyond doubt; another common and uncertain, which declares a thing probably. Moral constancy indeed commonly indicates that true doctrine is not alien to virtue; metaphysical constancy assigns to it the common affection of being; but neither is its proper sign or indication, by which it may be most certainly distinguished from false dogmas. Let us therefore call it a probable sign of truth, according to that old saying: a lasting criterion of truth. Yet we do not deny that true and saving doctrine is most constant, indeed eternal, as is clear from the sacred letters, Ps. 119, Matt. 5, Mark 13, Luke 15, 1 Pet. 1:23, 25. And this comparison, which Mühlhusius draws in these words, proves only so much: As it is necessary that the true Church of Christ be constant and the same and persevering, since it is founded upon a firm rock; so it is also necessary that true and catholic doctrine be not only ancient (for there are also very ancient heresies) but also one, the same, and constant and persevering. These things are indeed rightly said, but nevertheless they do nothing to show that constancy is a proper and undoubted sign of true doctrine, such as must be demanded of it altogether, if amid so great a variety of religions among Christians one wishes to choose the one prudently and safely.

units.la: Conclusio tertia est. Tantum abest, ut sola Romana doctrina, qua nunc est, sit constans, ut neque cum aliis aut inter alias constans sit. Hac conclusionem, Bellarmino pariter ac Mülhu-sino oppositam, ita accipe, ut sive Roma-nam papistarum doctrinam ad veterem illam à Paulo apostolo Romanis traditam compares, inconstantem plane ac apostati[?]am scias, sive ad secula ventura referas. nullum quoq; perpetuæ durationis privilegium præ aliis habere, sed certu ac meritissimū interitum[?] exspectare ex verbo Dei cognoscas. Romanam doctrinam inconstantiæ ju-re argui, ob defectionem à veteri Romana, paucis manifestum facio. Ita verus ecclesia docet de fide: Justus ex fide vivit. Vivit autem non amplius ille, sed vivit in eo Christus, & vitam quam nunc vivit Christus in carne, vivit per fidem filii Dei, qui dilexit eum, & tradidit semetipsum pro eo. Confer ad Rom. 1. 17. Rom. 3. 22. 28. & c. 11. 6. Adde ad Gal. 2, 16. ut omittam alia sexcenta scripturæ testimonia quibus antiqua Romanorum doctrina de ju-stificatione fidei defenditur, aliquot veteres ecclesiæ istius patres audite. Ita Hieronymus in c. 10. ad Rom. Deus ex sola fide justificat. Ita Ambrosius ad Rom. c. 3. Justificati sunt gratis, quia nihil operantes, neq; vicem reddentes, sola fide justificati sunt, dono Dei. Theodoretus in ep. ad Rom. Sola fide allata peccatorum remissionem accepimus, quoniam veluti quoddam redemptionis precium Dominus Christus suum corpus obtulit. Et lib. 7. de sacrificiis: Neque enim ullis operibus nostris, sed per solam fidem mystica bona consequuti sumus. Ita nobiscum sensit ac credidit olim antiqua ecclesia. Sed audiamus quantum distet hodierna
units.tr: Third conclusion. So far is the Roman doctrine as it now stands from being constant that it is neither constant with others nor among others. I ask you to take this conclusion, which is opposed to both Bellarmine and Mülhusius, in this sense: whether you compare the Roman doctrine of the Papists with that ancient one which the apostle Paul handed down to the Romans, you will know it to be plainly inconstant and apostate, or whether you refer it to the ages to come, you will learn from the Word of God that it has no privilege of perpetual duration above others, but awaits a certain and well-deserved destruction. That the Roman doctrine is charged with inconstancy, on account of its defection from the ancient Roman faith, I will show in a few words. Thus the true Church teaches concerning faith: "The just lives by faith. Yet he no longer lives, but Christ lives in him; and the life which he now lives in the flesh, Christ lives by the faith of the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him." Compare Romans 1:17; Romans 3:22, 28; and chapter 11:6; add Galatians 2:16. To pass over the other six hundred testimonies of Scripture by which the ancient Roman doctrine of the justification of faith is defended, hear some of the ancient Fathers of that Church. Thus Jerome, on Romans chapter 10: "God justifies by faith alone." Thus Ambrose, on Romans chapter 3: "They are justified freely, because, doing nothing and returning nothing, they are justified by faith alone, by the gift of God." Theodoret, on the epistle to the Romans: "By faith alone, when it is offered, we receive the remission of sins, since the Lord Christ offered his body as a kind of price of redemption." And in book 7 on sacrifices: "For we have obtained the mystical goods not by any works of ours, but through faith alone." Thus the ancient Church once felt and believed together with us. But let us hear how far the present papal doctrine is from this.

units.la: papana. Ita illa docet: Quod iustus ex fide vi-vit, illud non habet in Christo, sed ex operatio-nibus suis, Censura Colon. sol. 118. Item quod fides iustificat, illam formam seu vim non habet ex Christo, quem apprehendit & possidet, sed à charitate nostra, sol. 114. & 92. Vide Bell. l. 1. de iustif. c. 18. Haec meditare, quisquis es bonus, & compara, atq; intelliges hanc novam papæ doctrinam à veteri illa longius abesse, quàm distant æra lupinis. Haec autem basis est doctrinæ, quæ vigere debet in ecclesia. Unicum adhuc addam, ex quo apostasia Romanensium, ut ex ungue leo, dignoscatur, Vetus ecclesia de certitudine salutis in Christo consequendæ docet: Certam esse uniuscuiusque credentis electionem, vocationem, iustificationem ac salutem: firmissimam q; ac iustificantem fidem esse ejus, qui Christi servatoris mentem sibi applicat. Huic doctrinæ suppetit scriptura. Gal. 3. Ego vivo in fide filii Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Id Paulus de se cordatè. At in omnibus credentibus quantum ad hoc salutis obtinendæ ratio est eadem. Rom 4. Scriptum est propter nos, quibus imputabitur credentibus. Sed custos carceris dixit ad Paulum & Sylam: Domini, quid oportet facere, ut salvus fiam? At illi dixerunt: Crede in Dominum Iesum, & salvus eris tu & domus tua, Act. 16. Et generalis promissio missio ita sonat, Marc. 16. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit. Subscribunt patres. Ambrosius[?] de exitu & vita Theodosii: Nos, inquit, inhaeremus fidei ad animae nostrae inquisitionem: quoniam in hac fidei militiae te-stimonium consequuti sunt seniores nostri, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, & inde hereditatem fidei nobis reliquerunt. Et de poenitentia lib. 1. c. 10. Qui fidem habet, habet vitam aeternam: qui vitam habet, non est exclusus à venia. Omnis, inquit, qui credit in eum, non peri-bit. Quum omnis dicitur, nullus excludi-tur, nullus excipitur. Haec est vetus doctrina, sed quantum ab ea dissonet nova, quae-so audite. Ad fidem non est referenda certicu-jusdam privati hominis propria salus. Admodum enim incerta est privata hominum justificatio, multoque magis aeterna ipsorum salus. Quomodo igitur in his usque incertis certissima fides versabitur? Censur. Colon. 97. Bellarm. lib. 3. de justif. c. 3. Atq; ita constat, Romanam pontificiorum doctrinam esse inconstantem, quando ad veterem illam apostolicam com-paratur. Sed eam, quantum ad futura secula, perennem fore, nullisdum promissionibus Deiid nititur, aut saltem niti demonstratum est. Imo vero brevi, circumactis nempe fata-libus ipsius periodis, cariosum papatus regnū coelestis unius plagæ inflictu esse periturum
units.tr: It teaches thus: "That the just lives by faith, he does not have in Christ, but from his own works," Censure of Cologne, p. 118. Likewise: "That faith justifies, it does not have that form or power from Christ, whom it apprehends and possesses, but from our charity," pp. 114 and 92. See Bellarmine, book 1 on justification, chapter 18. Consider these things, whoever you are, and good luck to you; compare, and you will understand that this new doctrine of the Pope is further from that ancient one than the Ethiopians are from the stars. This, moreover, is the foundation of the doctrine which ought to flourish in the Church. I will add one more point, by which the apostasy of the Romanists may be recognized, as the lion is known by its claw: the ancient Church teaches concerning the certainty of salvation to be obtained in Christ: "The election, calling, justification and salvation of every believer is certain; and the faith of him who applies to himself the mind of Christ the Saviour is most firm and justifying." Scripture supports this doctrine. Galatians 2: "I live in the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me." Paul said this of himself, rightly. And in all believers the manner of obtaining salvation is the same in this respect. Romans 4: "It was written for our sake, to whom it will be imputed, who believe." But the jailer said to Paul and Silas: "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" And they said: "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your house," Acts 16. And the general promise of the mission sounds thus, Mark 16: "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved." The Fathers agree. Ambrose, on the death and life of Theodosius: "We, he says, cling to faith for the examination of our soul; since our elders, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, obtained this testimony in the warfare of faith, and from there left us the inheritance of faith." And on repentance, book 1, chapter 10: "He who has faith has eternal life; he who has life is not excluded from pardon. Everyone, he says, who believes in him will not perish. When it is said 'everyone', no one is excluded, no one is excepted." This is the ancient doctrine; but please hear how far the new doctrine dissents from it. "The personal salvation of a certain private man is not to be referred to faith. For the private justification of men is altogether uncertain, and much more so their eternal salvation. How, then, will the most certain faith dwell in things so uncertain?" Censure of Cologne, p. 97; Bellarmine, book 3 on justification, chapter 3. And so it is established that the Roman doctrine of the papists is inconstant, when it is compared with that ancient apostolic one. But that it will be perennial for ages to come, it does not rest on any promises of God as yet, or at least it has not been shown to rest on them. Indeed, soon, namely when the fated periods of the thing itself are completed, the decayed kingdom of the papacy will perish by a stroke of the heavenly plague, a certain hope.

units.la: certa spes est. Etenim papatus iam in præci-pitium vergit, defervescente͏q; illo superstitio-nis æstu ejus vigor marcescit, & illa simul de-ceptionis efficacia nonihil remittit, uti Dani-el prædixit cap. II. 4f. Et venit ad finem suum. Quò etiam Johannes oculum intendit, quan-do cap. 17. v. 6. post septem phialarum de-cursum mulierem producit ebriam sanguine sanctorum & sanguine testium Jesu, per quæ ei vertigo capitis oboritur, ut titubare incipi-at. Verùm quod ad primam incôstantiæ cau-sam, negant adversarii eam in Romanam, quæ hodie est, doctrinam competere, ut vide-re est in Bellarmino & Mülhusino. Bellarmi-nus ait: Iam vero constat ecclesiam nostram durasse ab initio mundi hucusq;, vel, si de statu novi testamenti loquamur, durasse à Christo hucusq; per 1577 annos, frustra eam oppugnan-tibus primò Iudæis, deinde paganis, ultimò hæ-reticis; nec solum durasse, sed etiam experse-quutionibus crevisse. Utrumq; falsum est. Ve-stra enim ecclesia nec duravit ab initio mun-di, neq; à tempore Christi. Nullus enim an-te Christi tempora, nullus etiá tempore Chri-sti fuit papa Romanus. At citra eum ecclesia vobis non est ecclesia vera, nisi male judicasti ac definivisti, Bellarmine, l. 3. de eccl. mil. c. 2, ubi ecclesiam dixisti cœtum hominum ejusdem Christianæ fidei professione, & eorundem sacra-menta.
units.tr: Indeed the papacy is already tending toward its fall; as that heat of superstition cools, its vigour withers, and at the same time that efficacy of deception somewhat slackens, as Daniel foretold in chapter 11, verse 45: "And he comes to his end." To this too John directs his eye, when in chapter 17, verse 6, after the course of the seven vials, he brings forward a woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the witnesses of Jesus, through which a giddiness of the head comes upon her, so that she begins to totter. But as to the first cause of inconstancy, our opponents deny that it applies to the Roman doctrine which exists today, as can be seen in Bellarmine and Mülhusius. Bellarmine says: "Now it is certain that our Church has endured from the beginning of the world until now, or, if we speak of the state of the New Testament, has endured from Christ until now for 1577 years, while Jews at first, then pagans, and finally heretics have vainly assailed it; and it has not only endured, but has even grown through persecutions." Both statements are false. For your Church has not endured from the beginning of the world, nor from the time of Christ. For there was no Roman pope before the time of Christ, and not even in the time of Christ was there a pope. But apart from him, by your judgment, the Church is not a true Church for you, unless you have judged and defined badly, Bellarmine, book 3 on the militant Church, chapter 2, where you called the Church a gathering of men bound together by the profession of the same Christian faith, and by the communion of the same sacraments,

units.la: mentorum communione colligatum, sub regi-mine legitimorum pastorum, ac precipue unum Christi in terris vicarii Romani pontificis. Ovum nempe fuit ante gallinam, & ante ovum pullus. Quis enim statim ab initio mundi in paradiso fuit Romanus pontifex? quis tempore Christi? At ecclesia tunc fuit vera. Vides ergo ecclesiam esse posse, imo fuisse, & esse sine capite vicario, Romano pontifice, quod nunc nihil aliud est, quam execrabile & immane antichristianismi monstrum. Sed hoc odoraris, ac dicis: Quamvis autem haretici huius temporis non concedant, nostram ecclesiam 1577 annos durasse; concedunt tamen durasse sine ulla interruptione a Gregorio I. hucusque, i.e. annos fere mille, quod tempus etiamsi solum esset, adhuc esset longius quam fuerit aetas ullius haeresis; sed tamen falsum est, non diutius durasse. Ipsi enim non possunt offendere per ullam historiam, aut veterum scripta, factam esse mutationem religionis in ecclesia Romana tempore S. Gregorii. Verum infirmitas huius argumenti varie patescit, atque ejus etiam peregrinitas. Antiquitas hoc argumento, si quid valeret, potius quam perpetua duratio probaretur. Sed de antiquitate jam pluribus egimus, & nunc quoque ex pontifice Romano Gregorio M. illis hoc corollarium addemus, qui l. 12, expos. moral. c. 15. pravam papistarum ium inrum indolem graphice depingit in haec verba:
units.tr: under the rule of lawful ministers, and especially of the one vicar of Christ on earth, the Roman pontiff. For surely the egg came before the hen, and before the egg the chick. For who from the beginning of the world was the Roman pontiff in paradise? Who was he at the time of Christ? Yet the Church then was true. You see, therefore, that the Church can exist, indeed has existed and exists, without a vicar head, the Roman pontiff, who is now nothing other than the execrable and monstrous monster of Antichristianism. But you catch a whiff of this and say: Although the heretics of this time do not grant that our Church has lasted 1577 years, they do grant that it has lasted without any interruption from Gregory I until now, that is, nearly a thousand years; and even if that period were alone, it would still be longer than the age of any heresy; yet it is false that it has not lasted longer. For they cannot point to any history, or to the writings of the ancients, showing that a change of religion was made in the Roman Church at the time of St. Gregory. But the weakness of this argument is manifest in various ways, and so is its novelty. Antiquity, if this argument had any force, would be proved rather than perpetual duration. But we have already treated antiquity at length, and now we will also add this corollary from the Roman pontiff Gregory the Great, who, in book 12 of his Exposition of Morals, chapter 15, graphically depicts the wicked character of the papists in these words:

units.la: Ut ea, qua afferunt, commendare stultis mentibus hominum quasi de antiquitate possint, antiquos patres se habere testantur: atq; ipsos doctores ecclesiae, sua professionis magistros dicunt: quumq; praesentes praedicatores despiciunt, de antiquorum patrum magisterio falsa praesumptione gloriantur: ut ea, quae ipsi dicunt, etiam antiquos patres tenuisse fateantur; quatenus hoc, quod rectitudine austruere non valent, quasi ex illorum auctoritate confirment. Idem sane ingenium hodie possident Jesuitae, quod olim in haeretica pravitate reprehendit Gregorius.
units.tr: So that they can recommend the things they assert to foolish human minds as if they had antiquity behind them, they declare that they have the ancient Fathers, and they call the very teachers of the Church, the masters of their profession; and while they despise the present preachers, they boast with false presumption of the teaching of the ancient Fathers: so that they confess that the Fathers held the things they themselves say, since by the authority of those men they confirm what they cannot uphold by rectitude. Indeed the Jesuits today possess the same disposition that Gregory once censured in heretical depravity.

units.la: 2· A Gregorii tempore non Romanam ecclesiam vere duraste, sed priscae illius idolu quoddam & larvam fuisse ut nunc est, concedimus. Quanta enim schismata in illa fuerunt, quorum etiam nonnulla ad centum fere annos duraste leguntur? Tres simul papae fuerunt; unus in Hispania, alter in Gallia, tertius in Italia, & nullus illorum legitimus est judicatus; omnes a concilio Constantiensi fuere damnati & exauctorati; sed ubi tunc fuit ecclesia Romana, sub uno Christi in terris vicario, pontifice Romano? In Utopia aut Cucagnia, ut nostrae quidem ecclesiae scoptice illudit Mulhusinus.
units.tr: 2. We concede that from the time of Gregory the Roman Church was not truly lasting, but was a kind of idol and mask of that ancient church, as it is now. For how many schisms were there in it, some of which are read to have lasted almost a hundred years? Three popes were at once: one in Spain, another in Gaul, a third in Italy, and none of them was judged lawful; all were condemned and deposed by the Council of Constance. But where then was the Roman Church, under the one vicar of Christ on earth, the Roman pontiff? In Utopia or in Cockaigne, as Mulhusinus mocks, scoffing at our Church.

units.la: 3· Etiamsi episcoporum successio ab eo tempore probari posset, id tamen nihil faene-raret papistis, nisi de doctrina pariter eam demon-
units.tr: 3. Even if a succession of bishops could be proved from that time, it would nevertheless profit the Papists nothing, unless they likewise demonstrated it in doctrine.

units.la: demonstrarent. Sed Æthnâ gravior hic eis labor erit. Nam Gratianus, tomi concilio-rum,aliiq; auctores luculerè docet, qui, quid, quādo & quantū in ecclesiâ invexerint, & pro- libidine mutârint. Talpâ cœcior sit, cui non videat in annos sua errores crementa habuis-se, alios atq; alios pontificibus noviter comminiscentibus. Mille annorum duratio, si ea in errores Romanos omnes congruat, non satis longa foret ad cōciliandum eis decus veritatis. Judaismus est antiquior, & gentilismus. Neuter verus, neuter verae religioni affinis. Quid ergo prae his habeat papismus? Id ergo concedas saltem, durationem non esse veram ecclesiae notam, quā tutō à falsis coetibus discernatur. Durant enim hi quoq; juxtā cum illa. Perge.
units.tr: They would demonstrate it. But this labour will be heavier for them than Etna. For Gratian, the compilers of the councils, and other authors teach plainly what, when, how much, and by whose authority they introduced into the Church, and how they changed things at their pleasure. A man would be blinder than a mole who does not see that errors have grown over the years, one after another, as the popes newly devised them. A duration of a thousand years, if it agreed with all the Roman errors, would not be long enough to win for them the glory of truth. Judaism is older, and so is heathenism. Neither is true, and neither is akin to the true religion. What then does Papism have over these? So concede at least this: that duration is not a true mark of the Church, by which it may safely be distinguished from false assemblies. For these also last alongside that one. Go on.

units.la: II. Deinde nostram ecclesiam esse veram ecclesiam probari potest etiam hoc argumento. Nam ante Lutheri tempora, non erant in mundo, nisi hæ religiones, paganismus, judaismus, Mahumetismus, Græcismus, Nestorianismus, Husitarum hæresis, & Romana ecclesia: Jed certum est non fuisse veram ecclesiam Christi apudullam ex prædictis, sed etiam Lutherani fatentur. Ergo fuit apud Romanam ecclesiam, aut certè periit de mundo omnis vera & visibilis ecclesia; quod non possefieri, supra docuimus, &c. Mirum, quā scientiā religiones ad tam pauxillas cōtrahere
units.tr: II. Next, it can also be proved by this argument that our Church is the true Church. For before the times of Luther there were in the world only these religions: paganism, Judaism, Mahometanism, Greekism, Nestorianism, the heresy of the Hussites, and the Roman Church. But it is certain that the true Church of Christ was not among any of the aforesaid, as even the Lutherans confess. Therefore it was among the Roman Church, or else every true and visible Church would have perished from the world; and this, as we have shown above, cannot happen, etc. What a wonder that with what knowledge you dare to reduce religions to so few,

units.la: audeas, quum non ignores, multò plures antiquitus exstitisse. Cur Arrianismi oblitus es? De illo Hieronymus contr. Luciferianos, quod nos hodie non immerito de papistis: Ingemuit totus orbis, & se Arianum esse miratus est. Vix quinque erant illis temporibus episcopi catholici, & verè Christiani, Athanasius, Hilarius, Eusebius Vercellensis, & pauci alii, uti ipse Stapletonus lib. 12. c. 18. fatetur. Nimium debilis quoque; est consequentia, quâ ab enumeratis religionibus fallis, ad papisticam vis transferre veritatem. Præterillas enim Romana ecclesia non fuit sola. Latitavit in illa & nostra. Nostra autem? Imò illa, de qua Athanasius in epist. ad solitariam vitam agentes in hæc verba scribit: Qua nunc ecclesia Christum liberè adorat? Siquidem ea sit pia est, periculo subjacet. Nam si alicubi sunt pii & Christi studiosi (sunt autem ubiq; tales permulti) illi itidem, ut magnus ille propheta Elias, abscondunter, & in speluncas & cavernas terræ se abstrudunt, aut in solitudine oberrantes commorantur. Huic ecclesiæ nos accensemus, huic nos adjungimus, quæ tamen, Dei beneficio, etsi sub persequutione jam clara satis esse cœpit. Quæ pia est, quæ Christi studiosa est, ejus membra esse & audire gaudemus. Nihil ergo est, quod nos ab illa invitos abstrahas, arceas. Nec tuâ, nec aliâ humanâ manu ex illa exscindi.
units.tr: when you cannot be ignorant that many more existed in antiquity. Why have you forgotten Arianism? Of it Jerome, against the Luciferians, said, which we today rightly say of the Papists: The whole world groaned and wondered that it had become Arian. At that time there were scarcely five Catholic and truly Christian bishops: Athanasius, Hilary, Eusebius of Vercelli, and a few others, as Stapleton himself confesses in book 12, chapter 18. Equally weak is the inference by which you transfer truth to the Papist religion from the false religions enumerated. For the Roman Church was not the only one among them. Our Church also lay hidden in it. But ours? Nay, rather that Church of which Athanasius writes in his letter to those living a solitary life, in these words: In what church now does one freely worship Christ? For if it is pious, it is exposed to danger. For if there are anywhere pious men and lovers of Christ (and such are very many everywhere), they likewise, like the great prophet Elijah, hide themselves, and withdraw into caves and cavities of the earth, or dwell wandering in the wilderness. We are counted in this Church, we join ourselves to it, which, by God's benefit, although already clearly enough begun to be under persecution. We rejoice to be its members and to hear it, since it is pious and a lover of Christ. Therefore there is nothing by which you may draw us away from it against our will, or keep us out. Neither by your hand nor by any other human hand can we be cut off from it.

units.la: L exscindi quimus. Et Græcismus melior eccle-sia fuit, quàm hodie est Romana. Esset ergo ac fuisset vera in terris ecclesia, licet Romana non esset, nec fuisset. Jam iterum perge. III.
units.tr: We cannot be cut off. And the Greek church was a better church than the Roman Church is today. Therefore there would be and would have been a true church on earth, even though the Roman Church is not and never was. Now again, go on. III.

units.la: Refert Theodoretus, in lib. de hæreticis fabulis, LXXVI. diversas hæreses usq; ad sua tempora exortas, & lib. 3. ejus operis testatur omnes illas exstinctas fuisse, paucissimis exceptis. Augustinus lib. de hæresib. numerat. 88. hæreses, ex quibus plurimas periisse testatur in expositi. Psal. 57. Nos numeramus usq; ad tempora Lutheri 200. hæreticorum diversissimas familias: ex his autem non superfuerunt nisi reliquiæ quædam Ne-storianorum & Eutychianorum in oriente; & Hussitarum in Bohemia, reliquæ omnes fundi-tus interierunt. Multa hic accumulantur, quæ discreté pervidenda sunt ac perpenden-da. Quid sequitur ex dicto Theodoreti? du-rationem esse notam ecclesiæ? [illegible, ~10 letters] Pleras q; hæreses antiquas evanuisse docet. Id credimus. Idem vult Augustinus. Audacis vero inexperientiæ crimine te obstringit judi-cium tuum ac calculus, qui ad Nestorianos & Eutychianos usq; omnem hæreticorum na-tionem periisse habet. Utinam vero omnes periissent! Deminuta quidem est Arianorum multitudo, non tamen prorsus deleta. Id lu-get Transylvania, id dolent multæ aliæ nati-ones. Quis nescit multos superesse tritheitas? [?] antitrinitarios? alios antiquae farinae hæreticos? Muhamedismum papismo coævum? Non igitur facile quis dixerit, omnes vetustas hæresesfunditus jam interiisse, nisi seculi sui ignarissimus. Quæ vero dira vaticinatis Lutheri, Zuinglii, Calvini doctrinas, ea inanilo-ga, vana, & temeraria judicamus. Futura e-nim & arcana Dei consilia, quæ verbo Dei ex-presa non sunt, citra peculiarem revelationem imprudenter asseruntur. Zuinglius Lutheri regnum, uti tu calumniaris, non attrivit; Calvinus Zuinglii doctrinam non represit ad pau-ca quaedam Helvetiorum oppida, sed Lutheri & Zuinglii pios labores in Dei gloriam & ec-clesiae salutem dilatavit, exornavit, & posteritati religiosissimè commendavit. Id monu-menta ipsius clare satis loquuntur. Neq; vero is etiam regnum sibi unquam apud Genevenses arrogavit, de cujus interitu anxiis solicitatur curis, sicut ex præfatione quadam Catechismi Genevensis, quem ad ministros in Frisia orientali misit, ariolaris, vel potius nequiter cavillaris. Non regno suo, quod nullum habuit, sed toti posteritati metuit, ob deplorandam sæculi ingratitudinem, qua cœlestis doctrinæ lucem oculis exclusit, sprevit,& per-sequutum est. Hæc sane cura omnes pios meritò solicitat, angit, cruciat, qui non omnino posteritatis securi perire[?] cupiunt, ac se pariter
units.tr: Theodoret reports, in his book on heretical fables, seventy-six diverse heresies arisen up to his own time, and in book 3 of that work he testifies that all of them were extinguished, with very few excepted. Augustine, in his book on heresies, numbers 88 heresies, of which he testifies that very many had perished, in his exposition of Psalm 57. We count up to the time of Luther 200 heretical families most diverse; of these, however, there survived only certain remnants of the Nestorians and Eutychians in the East, and of the Hussites in Bohemia; all the rest perished utterly. Many things are piled up here, which must be carefully considered and weighed. What follows from the saying of Theodoret? That duration is a mark of the Church? [illegible, about 10 letters] He teaches that most ancient heresies have vanished. We believe it. Augustine wills the same. But your judgment and reckoning, which holds that every nation of heretics has perished down to the Nestorians and Eutychians, binds you with the charge of bold inexperience. Would that they had all perished! The number of Arians has indeed been diminished, but not wholly destroyed. Transylvania mourns this; many other nations grieve at it. Who does not know that many Tritheites survive? [?] Antitrinitarians? Other heretics of the old stamp? Mohammedanism, coeval with Papism? Therefore no one could easily say that all ancient heresies have now utterly perished, unless he were most ignorant of his own age. But what dire things you prophesy of the doctrines of Luther, Zwingli, and Calvin, we judge to be empty, vain, and rash. For future and secret counsels of God, which are not expressed in the Word of God, are imprudently asserted without a special revelation. Zwingli did not wear down Luther's kingdom, as you slander; Calvin did not restrict Zwingli's doctrine to a few towns of the Swiss, but spread, adorned, and most religiously commended to posterity the pious labours of Luther and Zwingli, for the glory of God and the salvation of the Church. Their own monuments speak clearly enough about this. Nor indeed did he ever claim for himself a kingdom among the Genevans, concerning whose ruin you are anxiously troubled with cares, as you conjecture from a certain preface of the Geneva Catechism, which he sent to the ministers in East Friesland; or rather you wickedly cavil. He feared not for his own kingdom, which he never had, but for all posterity, on account of the lamentable ingratitude of the age, which shut out the light of heavenly doctrine from its eyes, despised it, and persecuted it. This care indeed rightly troubles, distresses, and tortures all the pious, who, not wholly secure about posterity, desire not to perish, and likewise not to lose that same doctrine.

units.la: & illam perdere. Verba Calvini sic habent, uti à teipso citantur: Dé posteritate ego sic sum anxius, ut tamé vix cogitare audeam, nisi enim mirabiliter Deus é coelo succurrerit, videre mihi videor extremam barbariem impendere orbi, atque utinam non paulo post sentiant filii nostri, fuisse hoc verum potius vaticinium, quàm conjecturam. Hæc fieri possunt, & tamen firmum manet spiritus oraculum, quo gaudet ecclesia nostra: Super hanc petram ædifica-bo ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferorum non præ-valebunt adversus eam. Quid enim aliud Calvinus cogitat aut dicit, quàm magister illius Jesus Christus ante prædixerat? Luc. 21. 17. Vos eritis exosi omnibus propter nomen meum. Et Joh. 16. 2. Ejicient vos ex synagogis suis; imo veniet tempus, quum quis quis trucidabit vos, putabit se gratum Deo obsequium præstare.
units.tr: The words of Calvin read thus, as you yourself quote them: I am so anxious about posterity that I scarcely dare to think of it; for unless God from heaven wonderfully comes to help, I seem to see an extreme barbarism hanging over the world; and would that our sons would not feel shortly afterwards that this was a true prophecy rather than a conjecture. These things may come to pass, and yet the firm oracle of the Spirit remains, in which our Church rejoices: Upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. For what else does Calvin think or say than what his master Jesus Christ had foretold before? Luke 21:17: You will be hated by all for my name's sake. And John 16:2: They will put you out of their synagogues; indeed the time will come when whoever kills you will think he is offering a pleasing service to God.

units.la: Haud dissimile est Hilarii de suo seculo augurium, qui in libro contra Auxentium, rarum esse ait, apud orientales invenire aut episcopum, aut populum catholicum, sed ubique scandala, ubique schismata, ubique perfidias. Hæ tales querimoniæ à piis doctoribus in tanta mundi pravitate non immerito ingeminantur, & omnibus seculis novantur. Universalia enim universaliter, particularia vitia particulariter solet Deus corrigere. Addis IV. Concludimus ergo cum S. Hieronymo in extremo dialogo adver-
units.tr: There is a similar prophecy by Hilary about his own age. In his book against Auxentius he says it is rare to find in the East either a bishop or a catholic people, but everywhere scandals, everywhere schisms, everywhere treachery. Such complaints are not unjustly repeated by pious teachers in so great a wickedness of the world, and they are renewed in every age. For God usually corrects universal evils universally and particular evils particularly. You add: "We conclude, therefore, with Saint Jerome in the final dialogue against..."

units.la: Brevem inquit, apertam animi mei sententiam proferam, in illa esse ecclesia permanendum, quae ab apostolis fundata, usque ad diem hanc durat. Et cum Augustino lib. de utilitate credendi c. 17. Dubitabimus, inquit, nos illius ecclesiae gremio concedere, quae ab apostolica sede per successiones episcoporum, frustra haereticis circumlatantibus, culmen auctoritatis obtinuit? Hieronymo non refragamur. Is permanendum censet in ecclesia, quae ab apostolis est fundata; nempe si & ipsa maneat in apostolorum doctrina. Secus in illa permanendum esse, non censuit Hieronymus.
units.tr: "I will state my opinion briefly and openly," he says, "that one must remain in that Church which was founded by the apostles and endures to this day." And with Augustine, in the book On the Advantage of Believing, chapter 17: "Shall we hesitate," he says, "to yield to the bosom of that Church which, through the succession of bishops from the apostolic see, has obtained the height of authority, while the heretics bark about it in vain?" We do not contradict Jerome. He holds that one must remain in the Church which was founded by the apostles, namely if it also remains in the doctrine of the apostles. Jerome did not hold that one must remain in a Church otherwise.

units.la: Jam vero pontificiam ecclesiam a fundamento apostolorum revulsam videmus & deflemus. Patiatur igitur nos fundamento a se relicto diutius haerere, & aeternum. Sed quid inde? An duratio est ecclesiae nota? Non, sed in vera doctrina perseveratio. Augustinus quoq; sententiae nostrae suffragationem meretur. Is enim hodiernum papae regnum nō attingit, sed florentissimam sui seculi ecclesiam a Donatistarum & Manichaeorum diverticulis longe lateque per orbem diffusam omnibus bonis commendat. Si vero etiam hodie tales episcopos, quales ab apostolo describuntur, quasi jure postliminii in ecclesiam Romanam revocetis, qui verbum Dei pure secent ac dispelcant, nos quoque lubentes ac gaudentes illos sequuti ad e-am redibimus[?]. Sed sic ad nos mutuo ibi-mus sub una veritate. Atq; ita rursus ex puri-oris doctrinae duratione, ecclesia rectius di-gnoscitur, quàm ex qualium qualium episco-porum perpetuata successione.
units.tr: Now indeed we see the Papal Church torn away from the foundation of the apostles, and we lament it. Let it therefore suffer us to cling for longer, and for ever, to the foundation it has abandoned. But what follows from this? Is duration the mark of the Church? No, but perseverance in true doctrine. Augustine also deserves to support our view. For he does not touch the present kingdom of the Pope, but commends to all good people the most flourishing Church of his own age, spread far and wide throughout the world, and away from the byways of the Donatists and Manichaeans. But if you now call back, as by the right of postliminy, into the Roman Church such bishops as the apostle describes, who cut and handle the word of God purely, we too will gladly and joyfully follow them and return to it. But thus we shall come to one another there under one truth. And so, again, from the duration of the purer doctrine the Church is more rightly recognised than from the uninterrupted succession of bishops of whatever sort.

units.la: Conclusio quarta est. Inter antiqui-simas haereses papismi colluvies eminet, Id olim adversus Jesuitam Moguntinensem asserui, necdum causam video, quae suadeat, ut defe-ram ac diversum sentiam, Ut a.[?] tibi sententiae mea occurrat vel non quaesita veritas, ita pau-cis habe. 1. Esse aliquas etiam haereses anti-quissimas, id Jesuita nobis largitur. Ex eo antiquitatem non esse certam ecclesiae verae no-tam supra confecimus. 2. Inter eas papismi colluviem EMINERE, i.e. amplitudine, mole ac noxitudine omnium pestilentissimam per-niciosissimamq; esse dico. Non fama dico, sed noxitudine sua oes alias haereses veteres supe-rare, ita ut ficum omnib. priscis comparetur, laevissima sit, & in antichristi malitiam tota degeneret atq; despumet. 3. Papismi colluviem dico, non primas ejus guttulas, non sca-turigines primas, non rivulum unum & alte-rum, sed totam illam, & putidam papistici sen-tinam & colluviem, omnes illas antichristia-nae doctrinae confluges, quae ex variis antiquis haeresibus per multorum saeculorum lapsum infelicitee[?]. infeliciter confluxerunt. Id ne papatui affingi à me conqueraris, ecce tibi luculenta hujus rei testimonia.
units.tr: The fourth conclusion is this: "Among the most ancient heresies the mass of Papism stands out." I asserted this formerly against the Jesuit of Mainz, and I still see no cause that would persuade me to retract or to think otherwise. So that my opinion may meet you, even if the truth is not sought, I will put it briefly. (1) That there are some heresies that are very ancient too, the Jesuit concedes to us. From this we have already shown above that antiquity is not a sure mark of the true Church. (2) I say that among these the mass of Papism STANDS OUT, that is, in size, bulk and harmfulness, it is the most pestilent and most destructive of all. I say that it surpasses all other old heresies not by reputation but by its harmfulness, so that it may be compared to a fig among all the ancient ones, it is most wicked, and wholly degenerates and foams over into the malice of Antichrist. (3) I say the mass of Papism, not its first drops, not its first springs, not one or another small stream, but that whole putrid sink and mass of Papism, all those confluences of antichristian doctrine which flowed together unhappily from various ancient heresies through the lapse of many centuries. Lest you complain that I am ascribing this to the papacy, here is clear testimony of the matter.

units.la: 1. Samaritani provocarunt ad traditiones quas à patribus suis acceperant, Epiph hæref.9. Papistæ accusant scripturas imperfectionis, & necessitatem traditionum non-scriptarum urgent. Vide enchirid. Cosleri[?] p. 47.
units.tr: (1) The Samaritans appealed to the traditions which they had received from their fathers (Epiphanius, Heresy 9). The Papists accuse the Scriptures of imperfection and press the necessity of unwritten traditions. See the Enchiridion of Cosler, p. 47.

units.la: 2. Nazareni dixerunt libros legis esse fi-ctos, Epiph. hærel. 18. Papistæ quærunt, unde sciamus libros Moisis esse Moisis? unde sciamus libros euangelistarum esse divinitus in-spiratos? qui sciamus eos non esse adulterinos & suppositiitios? Pighius[?] hierarch. eccles. lib. 1. c. 2. sol. 4.
units.tr: (2) The Nazarenes said that the books of the law were fictitious (Epiphanius, Heresy 18). The Papists ask: how do we know that the books of Moses are Moses'? How do we know that the books of the evangelists were divinely inspired? How do we know that they are not spurious and supposititious? Pighius, Hierarchy of the Church, book 1, chapter 2, solution 4.

units.la: 3. Basilidiani & Carpocratita celarunt doctrinam suam, ac dixerunt: Nos sumus homines, cæteri omnes sunt canes & porci. Ne ꝓji-cite[?] ergo margaritas porcis, & sanctum canib.
units.tr: (3) The Basilidians and Carpocratians concealed their teaching and said: "We are men, all the rest are dogs and swine. Therefore do not cast pearls before swine, and what is holy to dogs."

units.la: Et qui eos redarguebant ex scripturis, eos accusabant, tanquam non redarguentes, & auctoritate nulla valentes. Adde quod veritate non intelligere docerent, nisi eos, qui traditiones novisset, & veritatem non tradi p-scripturam, sed per vivam vocem. Vide Irenæum l.1.c. 2. & 3. Epiph. hær. 24. Papistæ haud sec loquuntur, quando laicos legere scripturas prohibent. Vide Albertum Pium in epist. ad Eras-mum. Ledesimam Jesuitam in lib. de scriptura.
units.tr: And those who refuted them from the Scriptures they accused as if they did not refute, and had no authority. Add that they taught that the truth could not be understood except by one who knew the traditions, and that the truth is handed down not by Scripture but by the living voice. See Irenaeus, book 1, chapters 2 and 3; Epiphanius, Heresy 24. The Papists speak no differently when they forbid the laity to read the Scriptures. See Albert Pius in his letter to Erasmus; the Jesuit Ledesma in his book on Scripture.

units.la: vernacula, Charron. c. 4. 3. verit. art. 4. Quid? quod Baronius annal. tom. 1. an. 33. sect. 11. ait, traditiones excellere scripturas, quod scripturæ non subsistant, nisi firmentur traditionibus: traditiones vero sine scriptura suam firmitudinem retineant.
units.tr: in the vernacular; Charron, chapter 4; Of Truth, article 4. And what of this, that Baronius, Annals, vol. 1, year 33, section 11, says that the traditions surpass the Scriptures, because the Scriptures do not stand unless they are confirmed by traditions, whereas traditions retain their firmness even without Scripture?

units.la: 4. Gnosimachi erant omnis scientiæ Christianæ adversarii, omnem e scripturis petitam notitiam respuebant, bona solum opera divinitus homini iusta docebant. Vide Damascenum de hæresibus. Papistæ asimilem in modum retrahunt vulgus à lectione scripturarum, commendant ei fidem carbonarii, dicentes: Fides tua te servat, non sensus in scripturis exercitatus. Vide Hof. de legit. Thucidides, lib. 2.
units.tr: (4) The Gnosimachi were opponents of all Christian knowledge; they rejected all knowledge sought from the Scriptures and taught that only good works are just before God. See Damascene on heresies. The Papists in a similar manner draw the common people away from reading the Scriptures, and commend to them a faith of the cobblers, saying: "Your faith saves you, not an understanding exercised in the Scriptures." See Hofmann on reading. Thucydides, book 2.

units.la: 5. Osfenii docuerunt jurare per creaturas, Epiphanius hæref. 19. Papistæ jurant per Mariam virginem & alios sanctos.
units.tr: (5) The Ossenians taught that one should swear by creatures (Epiphanius, Heresy 19). The Papists swear by the Virgin Mary and other saints.

units.la: 6. Carpocratita venerati sunt imagines Jesu, Pauli, Homeri & Pythagoræ, cum suffimentis eas adorarunt. Habuerunt imagines coloribus pictas, aureas, argenteas, alias, quas dicebant esse Jesu. Idem dictitabant Gnostici. Vide Augustinum de hæref. c. 7. Epiphanium hæref. 27, Irenæum lib. 1. c. 24. Papistæ idem faciunt, dicunt, habent.
units.tr: (6) The Carpocratians venerated images of Jesus, Paul, Homer and Pythagoras, and worshipped them with incense. They had images painted in colours, golden, silver and other images, which they said were of Jesus. The Gnostics kept saying the same. See Augustine, On Heresies, chapter 7; Epiphanius, Heresy 27; Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 24. The Papists do the same, say the same, and have the same.

units.la: 7. Cajani hæreseos sunt damnati, quod adorarint angelos. Epiphanius hæref. 38, Ideo dicti sunt Angelici. Papistae vulgariter invocant in genere omnes angelos, & nominatim suum quisque angelum custodem.
units.tr: (7) The Cainite heresy was condemned because they worshipped angels (Epiphanius, Heresy 38); hence they were called Angelici. The Papists commonly invoke all angels in general, and each one by name his own guardian angel.

units.la: 8. Armeniani adorarunt crucem. Unde & appellati sunt Chazinzarii & ftaurolatrae. Euthymius in panopl. Niceph. lib. 18, c. 54. Papistae crucem diserte adorant, ac dicunt, crucem tuam adoramus.
units.tr: (8) The Armenians worshipped the cross, and for this reason they were called Chazinzarians and staurolaters. Euthymius, Panoplia; Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 54. The Papists openly adore the cross and say, "We adore your cross."

units.la: 9. Iacobitae & Armeniani effigiarunt imagines Dei patris ac Spiritus sancti, id quod abfurdissimum est, teste Nicephoro lib. 18. c. 53[?]. Papistis tam solenne id est, ut nullum fere templum apud eos visatur, in quo Deus pater cana barba pictus, & Spiritus sanctus per columbam figuratus non inveniatur.
units.tr: (9) The Jacobites and Armenians made images of God the Father and of the Holy Spirit, which is most absurd, as Nicephorus testifies, book 18, chapter 53. With the Papists this is so common that hardly any temple is to be seen among them in which God the Father is not painted with a white beard and the Holy Spirit is not depicted by a dove.

units.la: 10. Agnus Christum repræsentans est figura Judæorum, juxta concilium Constantinopolitanum. Vide Caranzam summ. concil. c. 82. Concil. constantinop. 6. general. Idem est repetitum a concilio Nicæno 2. act. 4. Sed quid agno cereo in papatu preciosius? quid sanctius? Ita papistæ judaizant secundum concilium, blasphemi sunt secundum veritatem. Res clara est ex epigrammatis Andreæ Frufii Jesuitæ, qui ea sic claudit: Legimus Urbanum quintum pontificem maximum misisse ad imperatorem Græcorum[?] tres agnos Dei cum versibus infra scriptis, aut si-milibus[?].
units.tr: (10) The Lamb representing Christ is a figure of the Jews, according to the Council of Constantinople. See Caranza, Summary of the Councils, chapter 82; Council of Constantinople, the sixth general council. The same was repeated by the second Council of Nicaea, act 4. But what is more precious, and what more holy, in the papacy than the wax Lamb? Thus the Papists Judaize according to the council, and are blasphemers according to the truth. The matter is clear from the epigrams of Andreas Frusius, Jesuit, who closes them thus: "We read that Urban V, the supreme pontiff, sent to the Emperor of the Greeks three Lambs of God with the verses written below, or similar ones."

units.la: Balsamum in tera munda cum chrismatis unda, Conficiunt agnum quem do tibi munere magnum, Fonte velut natum per myslica sanctificatum. Fulgura desursum fugiunt ac omne malignum: Pragnans fervatur, proles fine vi generatur; Portantem tumida de fluctibus eruit unda: Peccatum frangit, crudeles damonas angit; Munera fert dignis, virtutem destruit ignis: Morte repentina fervat, fatanaq; ruina: Si quis honorabit, certa hosti damna parabit: Id virtutis habet pars parva, quod integer agnus.
units.tr: Balsam in pure earth with the water of chrism they make a lamb, which I give you as a great gift, born from the fount and sanctified by mystical rites. Lightnings flee from above and every evil thing; it is kept pregnant, and offspring is produced without violence; the swelling wave rescues it from the waves as it carries it; it breaks sin, and afflicts cruel demons; it bears gifts to the worthy, and fire destroys its power; it preserves from sudden death and from the ruin of Satan; if anyone honours it, he prepares certain loss for the enemy; this virtue has the small part, which the whole lamb has.

units.la: O idololatriam! o insaniam!
units.tr: O idolatry! O madness!

units.la: II. Collyridiani habiti sunt pro haereticis & idololatris, quod adorarint sanctam virginem in necessariis suis rebus, & ei placentas obtulerunt. Epiphanius haer. 79. Papistae eandem adorant, invocant, ei offerunt suffitus & candelas.
units.tr: II. The Collyridians were held to be heretics and idolaters, because they worshipped the Holy Virgin in their necessities and offered her cakes. Epiphanius, Heresy 79. The Papists worship and invoke her in the same way, and offer her incense and candles.

units.la: XII. Encratita in numerum suum non admiserunt uxoratos, neq; carnes ederunt, tanquam impuras. Idem a Tatianis facitatum est. Vide Augustinum de haeref c. 2 f. Papista-rum monachi quoq; non recipiunt uxoratos. Carthusiani non vescuntur carnibus. Et cau-lam[?], de qua non edunt carnes tempore quadragesimae & jejunii, allegant terrae maledictionem, Vide Durand. rational lib. 6. c. 7. Quis non videt eos ita cibos pro maledictis habere?
units.tr: XII. The Encratites did not admit married men into their number, and they ate no meat, as if it were unclean. The same practice was followed by the Tatians. See Augustine, De haeresibus, ch. 2 (f.). The monks of the Papists also refuse to admit married men. The Carthusians do not eat meat. And the cabbage(?), from which they do not eat meat during Lent and the fast, they justify by appeal to the curse on the earth. See Durandus, Rationale, book 6, ch. 7. Who does not see that they regard these foods as accursed?

units.la: XIII. Manichaei condemnarunt conjugium in electis eorum, vulgo autem permiserunt, Augusti. ep. 74. Papistae damnant conjugi-um sacerdotum & monachorum, in vulgo tolerant.
units.tr: XIII. The Manichaeans condemned marriage among their elect, but permitted it for the common people. See Augustine, letter 74. The Papists condemn the marriage of priests and monks, but tolerate it among the laity.

units.la: 14. Montanus jejunia fixa mandavit & fancivit, Eusebius lib. 5. c. 17. & scripturis assui voluit suas revelationes. Papistae hunc imitati de jejunio suo leges figunt & revelationes jactant.
units.tr: 14. Montanus ordained and enjoined fixed fasts. See Eusebius, book 5, ch. 17. He also wished his own revelations to be attached to the Scriptures. The Papists, imitating him, lay down laws about their fasting and boast of revelations.

units.la: 15. Nudipedales ponuntur in haereticis, apud Augusti. de haer. c. 68. Papistarum Capucini, & alii imitantur illorum superstitionem cum opinione meriti & satisfactionis.
units.tr: 15. The Barefoot ones are listed among the heretics, according to Augustine, De haeresibus, ch. 68. The Capuchins of the Papists, and others, imitate their superstition, together with the belief in merit and satisfaction.

units.la: 16. Priscillianistae matrimonia solverunt eorum, quibus haerefin suam persuaserant, eripientes foeminis suos maritos, & maritis suas uxores, Augusti. de haer. c. 70. Papistae docent per vota solennia solvi matrimonium ratum, non consummatum. Vide Bellarminum lib. 2. de monachis c. 38.
units.tr: 16. The Priscillianists dissolved the marriages of those whom they had persuaded to their heresy, snatching husbands from their wives and wives from their husbands. See Augustine, De haeresibus, ch. 70. The Papists teach that a consummated-not-yet marriage, a ratified one, is dissolved by solemn vows. See Bellarmine, book 2 on monks, ch. 38.

units.la: 17. Messaliani sibi fecerunt oratoria, in quibus cum cereis accensis convenientes mane & vesperi orabant, propriis bonis se abdicabant, saccis vestiebantur, & vicatim eleemosynas petebant, certasq; preces perpetuo deblaterabant, unde & Euchitae sunt dicti; peccata etiam praeterita per baptismum duntaxat aboleri, non futura. Vide Theodoret. & Epiph. decret. can. de bapt. Idem papistis est solemne.
units.tr: 17. The Messalians made for themselves places of prayer, in which they gathered morning and evening with lighted candles and prayed. They renounced their own goods, were clothed in sackcloth, and went from village to village begging alms, and they ceaselessly babbled set prayers; whence they were also called Euchites. They also held that sins committed before baptism are removed by baptism alone, and not those to come. See Theodoret and Epiphanius, Decretum, canon on baptism. The same is customary among the Papists.

units.la: 18. Helcesaitae preces fundebant ignora lin-gua. guâ, Epiphan. hæref. 19. Papistæ vulgó orant linguâ, quàm nec vulgus neq; etiam sacrificu-lorúm bona pars intelligit.
units.tr: 18. The Helcesaites poured out prayers in an unknown tongue. See Epiphanius, heresy 19. The Papists commonly pray in a tongue which neither the common people nor even a good part of the priests understand.

units.la: 19. Simon Magus obtulit apostolis pecu-niam, ut emeret dona Spiritus sancti, Act. 8. v. 18. Hoc ita usitatum[?] est papistis, ut proprii eorum auctores reticere nequeant:
units.tr: 19. Simon Magus offered money to the apostles, that he might buy the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Acts 8:18. This is so customary among the Papists that their own authors cannot keep silent:

units.la: — Venalia nobis
units.tr: — Venalia nobis

units.la: Templa, sacerdotes, altaria, sacra, corona, Ignis, thura, preces, cœlum est venale, deum q.
units.tr: Temples, priests, altars, sacred rites, the crown, fire, incense, prayers: heaven itself is for sale, and God too.

units.la: Verba sunt Mantuani lib. 3. de calam. suorum temp. Vide etiam Guicciard. hist. Ital. l. 1. §. 2. & Claudium Defpensæum, doctorem Sorbonicum, super cap. 1. ep. ad Titum, ubi, postea-quam detestatus est horrorem cancellariæ Romanæ, scribit:
units.tr: These are the words of Mantuan, book 3, On the calamities of his times. See also Guicciardini, Italian History, book 1, §2, and Claude Despence, Sorbonne doctor, on chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus, where, after he has denounced the horror of the Roman chancery, he writes:

units.la: — habeat jam Roma pudorem!
units.tr: — let Rome now have shame!

units.la: Idem etiam Simon tradidit purgationem animarum post hanc carnis nostræ vitam, ut est apud Epiphan. hæref. 21. Sic etiam papistæ tradunt purgatorium post mortem corporis.
units.tr: Simon also taught a purification of souls after this life of our flesh, as is found in Epiphanius, heresy 21. Thus the Papists too teach a purgatory after the death of the body.

units.la: 20. Marcionitæ permiserunt fœminis baptismum, Epiph. hær. 42. quod etiam fecere Peputiani, teste August. de hær. c. 27. Papistæ id similiter permittunt.
units.tr: 20. The Marcionites permitted women to baptize, Epiphanius, heresy 42, which the Peputians also did, as Augustine attests, De haeresibus, ch. 27. The Papists likewise permit this.

units.la: 21. Heracleonitæ unxerunt moriturientes oleo, cum certis precibus, uti est apud August. de hæref. c. 16. Jun. l. 1. c. 18. Papistæ extremam unctionem pro sacramento habent.
units.tr: 21. The Heracleonites anointed the dying with oil, with certain prayers, as is found in Augustine, De haeresibus, ch. 16. Junius, book 1, ch. 18. The Papists hold extreme unction to be a sacrament.

units.la: 22. Hemerobaptistæ se quotidie lavant aqua ad remissionem peccatorum, Epiphanius hæref. 17. Ita papistæ se aqua lustrali aspergunt ad remissionem peccatorum venialium, quæ vocant.
units.tr: 22. The Hemerobaptists wash themselves daily in water for the forgiveness of sins, Epiphanius, heresy 17. So the Papists sprinkle themselves with lustral water for the forgiveness of what they call venial sins.

units.la: 23. Manichæi ex eucharistia resecant symbolum vini, solùm distribuunt panè, Leo serm. 4. de quadragef. Papistæ similiter speciem vini populo eripiunt. Iidem Manichæi se egregiè credunt jejunasse, si abstinuerunt à carnibus, licèt se referciant piscibus, & aliis deliciis, Augustin. de morib. Manich. l. 2. c. 13. Quid aliud fit à papistis?
units.tr: 23. The Manichaeans withhold the sign of the wine from the Eucharist and distribute only the bread. Leo, sermon 4 on Lent. The Papists likewise take the cup away from the people. The same Manichaeans thought they had fasted admirably if they abstained from meat, although they regaled themselves with fish and other delicacies. Augustine, On the Morals of the Manichaeans, book 2, ch. 13. What is that other than what the Papists do?

units.la: 24. Eutyches existimavit carnem Christi eodem tempore esse in cœlo & in terra, Vigilius contra Eutych. lib. 4. Ita papistæ accidentibus panis includunt Christi corpus, quod jam est in cœlo.
units.tr: 24. Eutyches thought that the flesh of Christ was at the same time in heaven and on earth. Vigilius, against Eutyches, book 4. So the Papists enclose the body of Christ under the accidents of bread, though it is already in heaven.

units.la: 25. Circumcelliones trucidabant quos suæ sectæ nolle adhærere animadvertebant, Augustin. hæref. 69. Ita papistæ in Italia & Hispania excarnificant & truculentum in modum necant, qui dogmata eorum in dubium vocant. Luctuosissimū est parricidium Alphonsi Diazii Hispani, qui Johanni Diazio Hispano, fratri suo, Buceri, postquam ex Parisiensi Academia ad protestantium confessionem, uti papistica veriorem transiisset, socio, Neoburgi ad Danubium securim totis viribus in capitis partem dexteram infligi adusq; manubrium curavit, ut ille subito perruptis omnib. organis cerebri, nulla ederet voce, uti est apud Sleida-num lib. 17. ad ann. 1546. pag. 279.
units.tr: 25. The Circumcelliones slaughtered those whom they noticed were unwilling to adhere to their sect. Augustine, heresy 69. So the Papists in Italy and Spain butcher and kill in a savage manner those who call their doctrines into doubt. The most lamentable parricide was that of Alphonsus Diazius, a Spaniard, who had his brother, John Diaz, a Spaniard, a companion of Bucer, after he had passed over from the Paris Academy to the confession of the Protestants, rather than to the papal one, cause a sword to be struck with all his strength into the right side of the head, as far as the handle at Neuburg on the Danube, so that the other, suddenly, with all the organs of his brain broken, uttered no sound, as is recorded in Sleidan, book 17, year 1546, page 279.

units.la: 26. Cathari gloriati sunt de meritis suis, feq; aliis putiores iactabant, de quib. vide Isid. orig. lib. 8. c. 5. Papistae quoq; confidunt suis meritis, & eorum monachi munda omnia fœdant, In mundo merito sese habitare negant.
units.tr: 26. The Cathari boasted of their merits and bragged that they were purer than others. On these see Isidore, Origins, book 8, ch. 5. The Papists also trust in their merits, and their monks defile all things that are clean, they deny that they dwell in the world by merit.

units.la: 27. Pelagiani ausi sunt dicere, hominem justum esse in hac vita sine peccato. Augustinus lib. 2. de bono perfev. cap. 5. & infantulos, qui ante baptismum moriuntur, possessuros extra regnum Dei vitam fatis[?] felicem. Prior error est omnibus papistis communis, qui docent hominem posse perfecte servare legem Dei in hac vita. Posterior est Ambrosii Catharini episcopi Italici, in lib. de statu infant. parv. post hanc vitam, & Alb. Pighii in controv. 1.
units.tr: 27. The Pelagians dared to say that a man is just in this life without sin, Augustine, On the Gift of Perseverance, book 2, ch. 5, and that infants who die before baptism will possess outside the kingdom of God a life fairly happy. The former error is common to all Papists, who teach that a man can perfectly keep the law of God in this life. The latter is that of Ambrosius Catharinus, Italian bishop, in his book on the state of little infants after this life, and of Albert Pighius in controversy 1.

units.la: 28. Pelagiani dixerunt, hominem per opera naturae mereri gratiam, aut per bonum usum liberi arbitrii, Augustin. de hæref. c. 88. Papistae docent, animam hominis ante regenerationem per remotionem impedimenti, & bonam motionem adversus Deum mereri de congruo primam gratiam, Gabriel Biel dist. 27. concl. 4. l. 2.
units.tr: 28. The Pelagians said that a man merits grace through the works of nature, or through the good use of free will. Augustine, On Heresies, ch. 88. The Papists teach that the soul of a man, before regeneration, by the removal of the hindrance and a good movement against God, merits the first grace de congruo. Gabriel Biel, distinction 27, conclusion 4, book 2.

units.la: 29. Eunomius iterum docuit, peccatorum perpeperpetrationem atq; in iis perseverationem non nocere iis, qui fidem à se traditam amplec-tantur, Augustin. de haeref. c. 54. Papistae docent in ecclesia includi etiam reprobos, scelestos, & impios, & ut quis dici possit pars verae ecclesiae non putant requiri ullam internam virtutem, sed tantum exteriorem professionem fidei, & sacramentorum communionem, quae sensu ipso percipitur. Vide Bellarm. lib. 3. de eccles. milit. c. 2.
units.tr: 29. Eunomius again taught that the commission of sins and perseverance in them does no harm to those who embrace the faith handed down by him. Augustine, On Heresies, ch. 54. The Papists teach that even the reprobate, wicked and impure are included in the Church, and they do not think that any inward virtue is required for someone to be called part of the true Church, but only outward profession of faith and communion in the sacraments, which is perceived by the senses themselves. See Bellarmine, book 3 On the Militant Church, ch. 2.

units.la: 30. Ethnophrones, secundum Damascenum, sequuti sunt institura ethnicorum. Papistae sunt Ethnophrones in plerisq; cerimoniis suis. Accendunt enim meridie in templis suis cereos & candelas, paganorum de more, id quod Lactantius stultissimum judicat l. 6. c. 2. Ab iisdem mutuati sunt aquam lustralem, Bacchanalia, Ambarvalia, & similia, fatente etiam Baronio ad annum Christi 200. f. s. Ex hisce pauculis, benevole ac pie lector, facile cognoscis, quam à vero nihil absim, qui papisui [?] colluviem inter omnes antiquissimas haereses eminere, i. e. pestilentissimam esse olim dixi, necdum secus sentire aut dicere possum. Summa; quidam scite admodum comparatunt papatum oceano, in quem se omnia flumina exonerant. Ita enim omnes omnino haereses diversorum temporum, locorum, personarum in hanc grandem abyssum se effundunt.
units.tr: 30. The Ethnophrones, according to Damascene, followed the institutions of the heathens. The Papists are Ethnophrones in most of their ceremonies. For they light wax tapers and candles in their temples at midday, after the manner of the pagans, which Lactantius judges most foolish, book 6, ch. 2. From the same sources they borrowed lustral water, the Bacchanalia, the Ambarvalia, and similar things, Baronius also admitting it, year of Christ 200 and following. From these few points, kind and pious reader, you easily recognise how far I am from the truth, when I say that the papal filth stands out among all the most ancient heresies, that is, that it was once the most pestilential; nor can I think or say otherwise. In sum, certain men have very aptly compared the papacy to an ocean, into which all rivers discharge themselves. For in this way all heresies of different times, places and persons pour themselves into this great abyss.

units.la: Hæc contentio, quam multùm, si opus fit, amplificare possumus, hæreticæ papistarum pravitatis sufficiens documentum esse quit, a cujus lectione omnia ingenia, quibus rectum est judicium, in stupore prope dabit imprudentia eorum, qui nobis veterum sectarum turpitudinem objiciunt, quarum tamen ipsimet sunt fectatores & fautores.
units.tr: This argument, which we can amplify much if need be, may be a sufficient proof of the heretical depravity of the Papists. From reading it, every mind to which right judgment is granted will be almost stupefied at the imprudence of those who object to us the baseness of the ancient sects, of which they themselves are the followers and supporters.

units.la: Quis tulerit Gracchos de seditione quereties? Quod si hæc veterum & papisticorum errorū comparatio parit cordolium adversariis nostris, meminerint illi vulgati istius:
units.tr: Who could bear the Gracchi so often complaining of sedition? But if this comparison of the errors of the ancients and of the Papists produces grief in our adversaries, let them remember that common saying:

units.la: Qui quæ vult dicit, quæ non vult, sæpe audit. Sed quid ad hæc omnia dixerit Jesuita Mogū-tinensis! Meminerunt antiquissimarum hære-seon scriptores ecclesiastici complures: non pauci data opera omnes conquisitas posterorum prodiderunt memoriæ, ut Irenæus, Epiphanius, Augustinus, Philastrius, & alii, & cum minutiores etiam persecuti sint TOTAM PAPISMI COLLUVIEM quæ inter oës eminebat, praterierunt prio-res, tanto coeciores historici, quanto D. Schön-feldius oculatior. Vafra hic est Jesuitæ sophistica & audax medaciloquentia. Vafrities est, quando diligentissimi hæresîeon oppugnatores & rationarii inter alias papismi colluviem præteriisse dicuntur. Non n. plane neglexe-runt, sed in antiquis hæresibus fusicaturigines & rivos istius colluvieii confignarunt: nec tamen plane illam expresserunt, quoniam nondum ad justam amplitudine & profunditate excreverat. Aucta est multis malis & superstitionib. a tempore patrum in hunc usque diem.
