Et corrupto stilo mentem meam depravat, quando p eminet ille eminebat reponit, q. tota papatus colluvies jam patrum memoria confluxerit tota, non a subsequutis seculis accreverit, quorum tamen priꝰ falsum & a mente mea alienum, posteriꝰ ex mente mea & verisimu est. Si ergo injuria primas inter haereticos tenere papistas dixerim, quod eorum colluvies non sit diserte ex-pressa ab Irenaeo, Epiphanio, Augustino, Phi-lastrio, & aliis antiquis: quo vos meliore jure doctrinam Calvini, Zuinglii, Lutheri, & fi-milium haereseos damnetis non immerito quaesiverim. Eorum n. nomina apud praefatos do-ctores non leguntur. Verum Jesuitis quod li-bet, licet ac decet, ar si nobis, quod decet, ma-xime libeat, minime tamen licet. Tam iniquè comparata sunt hujus saeculi certamina! Neq; etiam video, qui se Jesuita ab audaci menda-cio liberet, quando D. SCHÖNFELDIUM, theo-logum in Academia Marpurgensi gravissimum, olim mihi praeceptorem perpetuo honore in Christo prosequendum sibi adversarium, & disputationis hujus auctorem parum oculatus fingit & insulse ridet. Sed is sibi tuedo sufficit.
units.tr: "He who says what he wishes often hears what he does not wish." But what the Jesuit of Mainz said to all this! "Many ecclesiastical writers have recorded the most ancient heresies: not a few have deliberately handed down to posterity the memory of all of them, as Irenaeus, Epiphanius, Augustine, Philastrius and others did, and although they pursued even the smaller ones, they passed over the whole sewer of Papism, which stood out above all the rest; the earlier historians were as much more purblind as Dr. Schönfeld is more keen-sighted." Here the Jesuit's sophistry is crafty and his lying bold. It is crafty when the most diligent opponents of heresies and chroniclers are said to have passed over, among other things, the sewer of Papism. For they did not altogether neglect it; in describing the ancient heresies they recorded the springs and streams of that sewer, though they did not portray it fully, since it had not yet grown to its proper size and depth. It has been increased by many evils and superstitions from the time of the Fathers down to the present day. He also distorts my meaning by a corrupted style, when he replaces "eminet" with "eminebat," as if the whole sewer of the papacy had flowed together entirely in the memory of the Fathers and had not grown in the following centuries. The first claim is false and alien to my mind; the second is from my mind and true. So if I had said unjustly that the Papists hold the first place among heretics because their sewer is not clearly expressed by Irenaeus, Epiphanius, Augustine, Philastrius and other ancient writers, then with better right you could be said to condemn the teaching of Calvin, Zwingli, Luther and similar heresies, and I would not unfairly ask why. For their names are not read in the aforementioned teachers. But the Jesuits may do whatever they please, and it is allowed and fitting; but if we do what is fitting, even if we very much wish it, it is by no means allowed. So unfairly are the contests of this age arranged! Nor do I see how this Jesuit can free himself from a bold lie, when, as a careless man, he pretends that Dr. Schönfeld, a most serious theologian at the University of Marburg, whom I once had as my teacher and whom I must honour with lasting respect in Christ, is his opponent and the author of this disputation, and he foolishly laughs at him. But Schönfeld is sufficient to defend himself.

units.la: Conclusio quinta. Reformata ecclesia fuit à mille sexcentis annis. Haec a. conclusio, ne cui absurda videatur, sapienter explica-da. Adversarii suam ecclesiam à mille sexcentis annis exstitisse frequenter & superbè crepant. Id a. quod sibi arrogant, de nostra ecclesia verius dici judico. Verum non consideranda est ecclesia sub actu & formalitate, ut sic loquar, reformationis, sed sub formalitate tum normae, ad quam post papismum est reformata, tum partium, quae integrae atq; purae fuerunt antequam tabes & pestis papismi in eam saeviret. Etenim tempore Christi & apostolorum ea reformatione, qua à papatu restituta est, nondum erat opus. nondum n. erat tantopere ab haeresiarchis deturpata. Norma a. reformationis jam tum erat, lex & testimonium, Ef.8. Partes etiam unius corporis, ecclesiae nempe Christi tunc erant aliquae, à quibus nos nec papae tyrannis nec tempora sive injuriae sive intervalla dividere possunt. Atq; haec causa est, cur olim dixerim Christi nunquam esse vidutum[?], nunquam sine sponsa, licet hac ipso-fam foris nigra & obscura faciat persecutiones antichristi: & licet quasi ad momentum derelicta videatur, miserationibus magnis a Deo congregari & Iesu denique cum ipsa Christianis usque ad consummationem seculi: sed id ita, ut non eodem modo & tenore id fiat, sed eam castiget, humiliet, purget, exerceat & intermissione aliqua magna illum & apparentis favoris, Dei finali[?] simul iustitia & misericordia illustretur, ut prae-clare docet Cyprianus lib. 4. epist. Haec non-dum revocare possumus, haec delere non audemus. Sed quid adhaec noster adversarius regerat audiamus. Sed quid haec omnia, inquit, sive Cypriani, sive Hilarii, sive Ambrosii, Catholicorum doctorum dicta Calvinianam sectam juvant? Si Christus nunquam viduum est, nunquam sine sponsa, permaneatq; cum illa usq; ad consummationem seculi. Fuit igitur hactenus [?]a mille & sexcentis annis sponsa ejus, i. e. ecclesia in orbe. Quanam illa? Calviniana. Ovum nimi-rum ante gallinam, et ante ovum pullus: fabula.
units.tr: Fifth conclusion: "The Reformed Church has existed for sixteen hundred years." This conclusion, lest it seem absurd to anyone, must be wisely explained. Our adversaries often and proudly boast that their church has existed for sixteen hundred years. I judge that what they claim for themselves is more truly said of our church. But the church is not to be considered under the act and form, as I may say, of reformation, but under the form both of the norm to which it was reformed after Papism, and of the parts, which were whole and pure before the corruption and plague of Papism raged against it. For at the time of Christ and the apostles, the reformation by which it was restored from the papacy was not yet needed; for it was not yet so greatly defiled by the heresiarchs. The norm of reformation was already then the law and the testimony (Isaiah 8). Some parts also of the one body, namely the church of Christ, then existed, which neither the tyranny of the pope nor the times, whether by injuries or intervals, can divide from us. And this is the reason why I once said that Christ has never been a widower, never without a bride, although the persecutions of the Antichrist make her outwardly dark and obscure, and although she may seem for a moment abandoned, she is gathered by God with great mercies and finally joined to Jesus with the Christians until the consummation of the age; but this happens not in the same manner and tenor, but He chastens, humbles, purges and exercises her, and by some great intermission the final favour of God is made clear together with His justice and mercy, as Cyprian teaches clearly in book 4 of his epistles. These things we cannot yet take back, nor dare we erase them. But let us hear what our adversary replies to this. "But what do all these things, says he, whether the sayings of Cyprian, Hilary, or Ambrose, Catholic doctors, help the Calvinian sect?" If Christ is never a widower, never without a bride, and remains with her until the consummation of the age, then up to now there has been for sixteen hundred years His bride, that is, the church in the world. "Which one then? The Calvinian." Forsooth, the egg before the hen, and before the egg the chick: a fable.

units.la: Superiori seculo natus (Calvinus est), ab eo tamen inventa religio mille & sexcentos annos ejus na-talem ante vertit. Res mira! Facundia Jesuitica plus quam canina est. Sectam Calvinianam, quam criminaris, patribus non opponere, sed ex vero & Dei verbo componere decebat.
units.tr: Calvin was born in the last century, yet the religion invented by him is turned back sixteen hundred years before his birth. A marvellous thing! Jesuitical eloquence is more than canine. It was fitting not to set the Calvinian sect, which you accuse, against the Fathers, but to compose it from the truth and the Word of God.

units.la: Quos enim ut Calvini sectatores traducis, Christi sunt & cupiunt esse imitatores, Christi sermonem audiunt, eundem à sanctis patribus repetitum, explicatum, applicatum non respuunt, sed cum observantia excipiunt.
units.tr: For those whom you slander as followers of Calvin are Christ's, and they desire to be imitators of Christ; they hear the speech of Christ, and they do not reject it when it has been repeated, explained and applied by the holy Fathers, but receive it with reverence.

units.la: Quid vero in argumentatione nostra desideras? Nempe Calvinianam ecclesiam dici sponsam Christi. Quare? quoniam Calvinus superiori seculo natus ante quatuordecim secula suam religionem fabricari non potuit. Belle! At
units.tr: What then do you miss in our argument? Namely, that the Calvinian church is called the bride of Christ. Why? Because Calvin, born in the last century, could not have fabricated his religion fourteen centuries before. Fine! But

units.la: quā tu traducis ut Calviniānam ecclesiā ea nihil credit, nihil amat, nihil observat à Calvino novè excogitatum, sola scripturæ oracula religiosè amplectitur: si quid lecus à Calvino doctum deprehendatur, id ipsa reprehendit, reicit, damnat.
units.tr: the church which you slander as Calvinian believes nothing, loves nothing, observes nothing newly devised by Calvin, but religiously embraces only the oracles of Scripture alone; if anything is found taught otherwise than by Calvin, the church itself reproves it, rejects it and condemns it.

units.la: Conclusio sexta.
units.tr: Sixth conclusion.

units.la: In tot & variis fortunæ fluctibus sola reformata doctrina & fides una eademq; per mille sexcentos hactenus annos à patribus ad nos propagata est. Ita in disputatione Marpurgensi scripsimus, & jam quoq; scribimus. Nē a mente nostra aberres, non id volumus quod sola reformata doctrina fuerit ab annis mille sexcentis; nullas verò hæreses, nulla falsa dogmata: (Id n. historiis repugnaret) sed hanc solam fuisse constantem, reliquas varias se. Id exprimimus verbis, una eademq;. Si quid n. ab antiquo Dei verbo discrepat, id omne ecclesia reformata repudiat. Cōstās igitur est, non varia ipsius doctrina. Adversarius tamē his ita oggannit. Addunt in variis fortunæ fluctibus solam reformatam doctrinam & fidem, unam eandemq; per mille & sexcentos hactenus annos à patribus ad nos propagatam esse. Quod cui rīsum nō moveat, Crasso severior est. A quibus enim obsecro patribus doctrina nostra ad nos usq; propagata est? Quis ex tanto numero ejus doctrinæ vel unico verbulo commemminit? & quū passim Romana depradicent, cur tātūm de refor-
units.tr: Amid so many and varied waves of fortune, the reformed doctrine alone, and one and the same faith, has been handed down from the Fathers to us through sixteen hundred years until now. Thus we wrote in the Marburg disputation, and we still write so now. Lest you wander from our meaning: we do not mean that the reformed doctrine alone has existed for sixteen hundred years, with no heresies and no false dogmas (for that would contradict the histories), but that this doctrine alone has remained constant, while the others have varied. We express this with the words one and the same. For if anything differs from the ancient Word of God, the reformed Church rejects all of it. It is therefore clear that its doctrine is not varied. Yet the adversary sneers at this in these words: They add that amid the varying waves of fortune the reformed doctrine and faith alone, one and the same, have been handed down from the Fathers to us through sixteen hundred years until now. Who would not laugh at this? It is more severe than Crassus. From which Fathers, I beg you, has our doctrine been handed down to us even to the present? Who out of so great a number has made mention of that doctrine even in a single word? And while you everywhere proclaim the Roman doctrine, why only of the reformed

units.la: Risus Jesuitæ est Sanctus donius, aut Ajacis. Equibus patribus doctrina nostra fuerit propagata, liquidum est. Præ- gressa disputatio id duobus exemplis oftedit / Vincentii nempe, & Augustini. Aliorum patrum scripta, quotquot integra, & scripturis consentanea doctrinam nostram propagant.
units.tr: The Jesuit's laughter is that of Sanctus Donius, or of Ajax. From which Fathers our doctrine has been handed down is clear. The preceding disputation showed this by two examples, namely Vincent's and Augustine's. The writings of the other Fathers, as many as are extant and agree with the Scriptures, hand down our doctrine.

units.la: Romana doctrina, quam patres deprædicant, non est papismi illa colluvies, quæ vetustissimam nunc orbem inundat / sed Paulinis literis notata. Reformatam quidem doctrinam patres non diserte nominant, quoniam eorum tempore papistarum violentia reformationem doctrinæ nondum piis doctoribus extorseras: doctrinam tamen ipsam luculenter tradiderunt, quam ecclesiarum reformatarum confessiones hodie tuentur. Hoc alii alibi operosius demonstrarunt.
units.tr: The Roman doctrine, which the Fathers proclaim, is not that heap of Papism which now floods the world, but the doctrine marked by the Pauline letters. The Fathers do not expressly name the reformed doctrine, because in their time the violence of the papists had not yet forced the reformation of doctrine from pious teachers; nevertheless they set forth the doctrine itself clearly, and it is what the confessions of the reformed churches defend today. Others have demonstrated this at greater length elsewhere.

units.la: Conclusio septima. Constantiam doctrinæ nostræ probamus ex scriptura sacra.
units.tr: Seventh conclusion. We prove the constancy of our doctrine from holy Scripture.

units.la: Sensus conclusionis est, nos ex sacrarum literarum perpetuo tenore ac sensu evidenter ostendere, nihil novi, nihil sicti continere doctrinam ecclesiæ, quæ a papatu recepit ac secrevit. Ratione attulimus hanc, quod scripturam sacram incolumem habemus. Firmum judico argumentum. Quæ ecclesia scripturam sacram habet incolumem, ejus doctrinæ constantia ex scripturis probatur. Atqui ecclesia reformata s. scripturam habet in colurnem. Ergo. Quid enim Eo ipso doctrina est constans, quod solu Dei verbum integre amplectitur. Jam vero eccle- siae reformatae id omne sunt damnare promta paratasq; , quod praeter & contra Dei verbum tanquam ad salutem necessarium docetur. Je- suita regerit. Omnia falsa. Et dilaniasti scri- pturas foedissime, quod in thesi 13. reservo, & e- jus sensum sacrilege pervertisti, quod thesis 14. monstrabit. Bona verba! Nempe Jesuita di- cit, & omnia falsa sunt quae dicimus. Sed qui- nia hoc caput differs in alium locum, nos quoque ibi sequemur, ubi foeditates vestras, & sacri- legia, q nobis criminose ac caluniose impingi- tis, vestrae esse clare demonstrabimus. Nos sa- cram scripturam integre legimus, sensum ve- ro etiam scripturae cum religione retinemus, quicquid oblatret os maledicum.
units.tr: The sense of the conclusion is that we clearly show from the unbroken tenor and meaning of the sacred letters that the doctrine of the Church, which it received and separated from the papacy, contains nothing new and nothing invented. Our reason for this is that we have holy Scripture intact. I judge the argument firm: the doctrine of the Church which has holy Scripture intact is proved constant from the Scriptures. But the reformed Church has holy Scripture intact. Therefore... For doctrine is constant by the very fact that it embraces the Word of God whole and entire. Indeed, the reformed Churches are ready and prepared to condemn everything that is taught as necessary to salvation beside and against the Word of God. The Jesuit replies: All false. And you have most foully torn the Scriptures, which I reserve for thesis 13, and you have sacrilegiously perverted their sense, which thesis 14 will show. Fine words! Indeed the Jesuit says that everything we say is false. But since he defers this point to another place, we too will follow him there, where we will clearly demonstrate that the foulnesses and sacrileges which you accuse us of, slanderously and falsely, are in fact your own. We read holy Scripture entire, and we keep its sense with reverence, whatever the slanderous mouth may bark.

units.la: Conclusio octava. Praeconium doctrinae reformatae publicum injuria temporum & ma- litia crudelissimorum hostium aliquamdiu fuit in sylvas, in montes, in carceres compactu. Haec conclusio iam demonstratu est facilis, postquam reformatam doctrinam nullam agnoscimus aliam, quam quae verbo Dei scripto per omnia, iis quae ad cultum Dei & salutem hominis praecipue sunt necessaria, exacte respondeat. Talem a. eam esse fanste affirmamus, vere credimus, constanter docemus. De hujus doctrinae perse
units.tr: Eighth conclusion. The public proclamation of the reformed doctrine was for a time driven into the woods, the mountains and the prisons, by the injury of the times and the malice of the most cruel enemies. This conclusion is now easy to demonstrate, since we acknowledge no reformed doctrine other than that which exactly corresponds, in all things pertaining especially to the worship of God and the salvation of man, to the Word of God written. We solemnly affirm that it is such, we truly believe it, and we constantly teach it. Concerning the persecution of this doctrine...

units.la: Perfequutione queritur scriptura, succlamant[?] historiae & patrum scripta. Scriptura quidem ad Heb. 11. ita tradit: Alii rursus ludibria & flagella sunt experti, insuper & vincula & carcerem. Lapidati sunt, disseäti sunt, tentati sunt, gladio caesi, mortui sunt, circumierunt cum evil-lis & caprinis pellibus destituti, afflicti, male habiti. Quibus indignum erat mundus, in desertis errantes, & montibus ac spelunceis, & cavernis terrae, &c. Horum fidem nos sequimur, horum doctrinam hodie defendimus. Historiae narrant persecutiones, & patres tyrannidem antichristi deplorant. Hoc mordet adversarium. Quapropter prae dolore exclamat: Quid haec omnia sive Cypriani, sive Hilarii, sive Ambrosii, catholicorum dicta Calvinianam sectam juvant? Juvant certe plurimum. Ex iis enim costare poterit quibus machinis publicum euangelii praeconium fuerit aliquamdiu praepeditum. Quare ea hic iure repetimus. Praeclare Hilarius contra Auxentium: Male vos, inquit, parietum amor coepit: male ecclesiam Dei in tectis, adificiis veneramini. Anne ambiguum est in iis Antichristum esse fesurus? Montes mihi & sylva & lacus et carceres & voragines sunt tutores, in illis prophetae prophetabunt. Commode Ambrosius lib. 4. Hex. c. 8. scribit: Ecclesiarum veteris tum novi testamenti sicut & huius, defectus habet & ortum frequentes: puta quod ad externam faciem, nō quod ad essen-tiam attinet. Repeto, quod olim scripsi, varias vices ecclesiæ nostræ ex Eusebio, Hieronymo, Ruffino, Socrate, Theodoreto & antiquioribus omnibus nos declarare, qui de Romana, quæ nunc est papatui serva, doctrinâ nullas laudes narrant. Adsit & explicetur catalogus testium veritatis, evolvantur martyrologia, & prodibunt patroni doctrinæ nostræ h.e. evangelicæ veritatis innumeri. Verùm Jesuita hæc more suo cavillatur & ridet in hæc verba: Amabo te, Schönfeldi, in quam sylvam? Arduennam vel Hercyniam? Semanam vel Vitulaniam? Quibus vero in montibus doctrinæ vestræ deformata præconium resonuit? in alpibus vel olympo? Parnasso vel Gargano? Vogeso, aut certè Meliboco? Qui tandem sunt tyranni, qui in vestra doctrina confessores ab annis mille sexcentis tantopere sævierunt? Utopia nimirum reges crudelissimi. Nullus & nemo. Deum immortalem! Quas fidiculas, ungulas, laminas, mamellas, olim experti non sunt Calviniani? Quas manicas, virgas, catastas non sanctificarunt? Quos eculeos, nervos, cippos, compedes, laqueos, suo cruore non tinxerunt? Testantur hoc per Christianum orbem ab illis excitata basilica et monumenta, quibus ipsorum martyrum cineres sacri conduntur & ossa. Testantur in illorum memoriam erecta statuæ, & arden-
units.tr: Scripture complains of persecution, and the histories and the writings of the Fathers cry out. Scripture indeed relates in Hebrews 11: Others again experienced mockings and scourgings, moreover also chains and prison. They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, they were tempted, they were slain with the sword, they went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated. Of whom the world was not worthy, wandering in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth, etc. We follow their faith; we defend their doctrine today. The histories relate the persecutions, and the Fathers lament the tyranny of antichrist. This bites the adversary. Therefore in his grief he cries out: What do all these things, whether of Cyprian, or Hilary, or Ambrose, the Catholic sayings, help the Calvinist sect? They help very much indeed. For from them it can be gathered by what machines the public proclamation of the gospel was for a time hindered. Therefore we rightly repeat them here. Hilary admirably, against Auxentius: Ill, he says, has love of walls begun to bind you: ill do you venerate the Church of God in roofs and buildings. Is it doubtful that Antichrist will make his lair in these? Mountains, woods, lakes, prisons and chasms are my guardians; in them the prophets will prophesy. Ambrose, in book 4 of the Hexaemeron, chapter 8, writes fittingly: The churches, both of the Old and of the New Testament, as also of this one, have frequent defects and origins: namely as regards the outward appearance, not as regards the essence. I repeat what I wrote before: from Eusebius, Jerome, Rufinus, Socrates, Theodoret and all the older writers we show the varied fortunes of our Church, who relate no praises at all of the Roman doctrine which now serves the papacy. Let the catalogue of the witnesses of the truth be brought forward and explained, let the martyrologies be unrolled, and innumerable defenders of our doctrine, that is, of evangelical truth, will come forth. But the Jesuit, after his manner, jeers at these things and says: Pray tell me, Schönfeld, into which forest? The Ardennes or the Hercynian? The Semana or the Vitulania? In which mountains has the proclamation of your deformed doctrine resounded? In the Alps or Olympus? Parnassus or Garganus? The Vosges, or at least Meliboceus? Who at last were the tyrants who raged so greatly against the confessors of your doctrine for sixteen hundred years? Surely cruel kings of Utopia. None at all, no one. Immortal God! What thumbscrews, claws, plates, pincers, have the Calvinists not once experienced? What manacles, rods, stakes have they not consecrated? What racks, sinews, stocks, fetters, nooses have they not stained with their blood? Basilicas and monuments raised by them throughout the Christian world bear witness to this, in which the ashes and bones of the martyrs themselves are kept holy. Statues erected in their memory bear witness, and...

units.la: Ardentis fidei testimonia, suspensi ante aras ipso-rum lychni. Testantur sacra vestes, in quibus auro, argento, gemmisq; contexta illorum vi-suntur effigies. Demum calices, patellæ, & quic-quid apud ipsos sacrum est, ipsi etiam templo-rum parietes & fenestræ clamant, quot quamq; insignes & viri et fœmina pro Calviniana fide et doctrina vitam & sanguinem profuderint. O-mitto fastos ecclesiasticos, qui illorum tatum cœ-litū nomina recensent, qui Lutherana, Swenckfeldiana, aut certe Calviniana religioni sese addixissent in terris. Antiquum obtinet Jesuita.
units.tr: Testimonies of burning faith, lamps hung before their altars. Sacred vestments bear witness, in which their images are seen woven in gold, silver and gems. Finally, chalices, dishes, and whatever is holy among them, the very walls and windows of their temples cry out how many and how distinguished men and women have poured out their life and blood for the Calvinist faith and doctrine. I omit the ecclesiastical calendars, which recount the names of all those heavenly ones who, while on earth, had devoted themselves to the Lutheran, the Swenckfeldian, or at least the Calvinist religion. The Jesuit maintains his old habit.

units.la: Posticis sannis addit jam anticas quibus nos ia-os illudit: sed eas procul dubio satanæ, ut li-ctoris Dei, tandem aliquando digne pinset ciconia, ut Persii verbo utar. Quid? miseria illusoris deflenda potius, quam talionis jure ulciscenda, Sylvas, montes, tyrannos, fidi-culas, ungulas, laminas, mamellas, manicas, virgas, catastas, eculeos, nervos, cippos, com-pedes, laqueos, quos pii martyres nostri & veritatis confessores experti sanctificarunt, & cru-ore suo tinxerunt, non modo Germania no-stra habet, sed & Gallia, Anglia, Scotia, Flan-dria, Brabantia, Italia, Hispania, Portugalia, America ipsa. Ne longus sim, abisis ad martyrologium magnum, primitus Gallica lingua postea vero in vernaculam nostram olim à D. Paulo Grotio, patre meo, jam inter cœlites sesundùm[?] meliore fui partem beato, exea tra-latum, & Hanoviæ editum anno 1606. Idy-rannidem papatus vestri, & constantiam martyrum nostrorum, ab apostolorum tempora ad nostrum usq; seculum, luculenter descri-bit. Id in ruborem dabit, aut potiùs in pallo-rem Jesuitæ impudentiam & audaciam, quā tot pios ecclesiæ nostræ martyres à suis impiè & crudeliter enectos ludificatur, nafoq; sus-pendit adunco.
units.tr: With the back of his jeers he now adds the old ones with which he mocks us; but these, no doubt, the stork will at last worthily pinch off for Satan, as the rod of God, to use the word of Persius. What? The wretchedness of the mocker is to be lamented rather than avenged by the right of retaliation. Forests, mountains, tyrants, thumbscrews, claws, plates, mamelukes... (sic) manacles, rods, stakes, racks, sinews, stocks, fetters, nooses, which our pious martyrs and confessors of the truth have experienced, consecrated and stained with their blood, are not only in our Germany, but also in France, England, Scotland, Flanders, Brabant, Italy, Spain, Portugal, and America itself. Not to be long, I refer you to the great martyrology, first published in the French language and afterwards translated into our vernacular by the late Dr. Paul Grotius, my father, now happily among the heavenly ones, and published at Hanau in the year 1606. It describes luculently the tyranny of your papacy and the constancy of our martyrs from the times of the apostles down to our age. This will bring a blush, or rather a pallor, to the impudence and audacity of the Jesuit, by which he mocks the many pious martyrs of our Church, impiously and cruelly put to death by their own people, and sneers at them with a hooked nose.

units.la: Etsi a. eorum cineres non as-servemus, ne plebeculæ novas superstitionum illecebras, & posteris peccandi illices conda-mus, nihil tamen ex iis perditum iri fides chri-stiana ex Dei verbo novit. Quid de ba filicis perChristianum orbem excitatis, & monimé-tis? Non certè omnes illæ à vobis sunt excita-se, & si essent, quid iuvaret id vestram perfidi-am, Simoniam vestram? Nostris quid (Sarra-dus Celtes primus Germaniæ poëta coronatus in vos scripserit?
units.tr: Even though we do not keep their ashes, lest we set up new superstitious allurements for the common people and entice later generations to sin, the Christian faith knows from God's Word that nothing of them will perish. What of the bonfires lit across the Christian world and the warnings they give? Surely not all of those were kindled by you; and even if they were, what would it help your perfidy and your simony? What does Sarradus Celtes, the first poet crowned in Germany, write against you in our time?

units.la: Vendit Roma Deum, vendit sacra, vendit honores,
units.tr: Rome sells God, sells sacred things, sells honours,

units.la: Et pœnam & culpam venialis tesserà tollit.
units.tr: And by the tessera of a venial sin takes away both punishment and guilt.

units.la: Exstant etiam in Alexandrum sextum papam vestrum hi versus:
units.tr: These verses also survive against your pope Alexander VI:

units.la: Vendit Alexander sacra, templa, altaria, Christum, Emerat ipse primus. vendere iure potest. Vestra an fidem accelsatur erecta statuæ, su-spensi[?] spensi ad aras lychni. Totidem superstitio-nis vestrae signa ostenditis. Statuæ contra Dei verbum Exod. 20. eriguntur, idololatriæ magistræ, alumnæ, columnæ. Quare sacrilegi decalogum mutilatis, secundum præceptum de idolis nec faciendis neq; colendis expungitis? Ira enim in officio Mariæ virginis, quæ sunt hodie Romanis usitatæ/tam Latine quàm Gallicè impressæ Lutetiæ Parisiorum cum privi-legio Papæ Sixti V. & correctæ jussu Pii V. præ-cepta leguntur: Non habebis deos alienos coram me, Non assumes nomen Domini tui in vanum. O sacrilegium! Damnant hoc sancti patres, qui idola sive statuas & imagines conflari prohibent (idolum enim & imaginem pro æquipollentibus habent ipsi quoq; pontificii, Cajetanus cardinalis in c. 20. Exodi, & Durandus episcopus rationali lib. 1. c. 3. cum Isidoro de origin. c. 11.) Clemens Alexandrinus lib. 1. & 5. stromatum, Eusebius lib. 3. prap. evangelica. Athanasius in orat. contra Greg. Sabell. omnes adeo usq; ad Damascenum lib. 4. de orthod. fide. c. 17. ut etiam Bellarminus lib. 2. de imag. c. 8. Durandu, in 4 Deut. q. 5. Peresiū de traditionib. parte 3 in tract de imaginib. Abulensem & patres nobiscum facere fatentur. Aræ quoq; non ad novum, sed ad vetus testamentum pertinent, si proprie, non a, figurate loquaris, Aræ n. respectant victimas. Antiqtas vero figurate tabulas ligneas quoq; dixit aras. Ita Athanasius de Arianis ligneas tabulas comburetibus queritur in epistola ad solitariam vitam agentes. Vide etiam Optatum adversus Parmen. lib. 6. Augustinus de verbis Domini secundum Iohan. serm. 46. Lychnos porro meridiano foli oppositos vis de veritate religionis tuae testari? Prudenter admodum & pudenter. Veteres usi sunt lychnis. Verum, necessitate, non voluntate cerimoniam religioni affingente. Recté n. Plinius de illis testatur lib. 10. ep. 97. ad Trajanum: Soliti erant stato die ante lucem convenire. Eodem redit Jesuitarum jactantia, qua nos negare non posse Christum ad candelam instituisse cœnam, ajunt. Instituit n. eam, ea nocte qua proditus est, 1. Cor. 11. De prisco more, vide Epiphanium lib. 9. tom. 2. Hieronymus contra Vigil. c. 7. Non accendimus, inquit, cereos interdiu, quemadmodum tu frustra calumniaris. Adhibemus lumina, ut temperamentum tenebrarum, ut vigilemus ad lucem, ne in tenebris tecum dormiamus. Lactantius etiam Firmianus hac de re scribit lib. 6. c. 62, quanquam Antonius Raudensis in indice errorum, id inter Lactantii errores referat, orthodoxi patris oppugnator papisticus, paganorum patronus, quem etiam Seneca, homo ethnicus, si viveret, non immerito rideret, verbis ex libro suo de beata vita c. 27. repetitis: Quum aliqua per viam repens ululat: laurumq; linteatus senex, & medio lucernam die praeferens, conclamat, iratum aliquem deorum, concurritis & audite, & divinum esse eum, invicem mutuum alentes stuporem, affirmatis. Porro ostentat Jesuita sacras vestes, in quibus auro, argento, gemmisq; contextæ visuntur effigies. At religio admittit suam majestatem, quando admittit simplicitatem. Vestium splendor est novus, non vere antiquus. Valafridus Strabo de rebus ecclesiasticis c. 24. testatur principio missam (ita illo seculo eucharistiam vocabant) celebratam fuisse in vestitu vulgari, quomodo etiamnum de quibusdam in oriente dicitur. Ridiculus vero sacrificorum habitus cum superstitione tandem auctus est. Legatur Tertullianus in libro de pallio: & imprimis Papa Coelestinus ep. 2. ad episcopos Gallicanos c. 1. in qua superfluam illam vestium vanitatē (falsē ridet, & docet doctores a populo discerni debere doctrinā, non tunicā; vitā, non habitu; puritate intellectus, non cultu corporis. Missis vestibus, calices tamen, patellæ, templorum, parietes, fenestræ clamant, quot quamq; insignes & viri et femina pro Calvinianâ fide & doctrinâ vitam & sanguinem profuderunt, ut habet scomma Jesuiticum. Sanctiores sunt nobis martyres nostri, quàm quorū nomina vestrā...
units.tr: Alexander sells sacred things, temples, altars, Christ himself; he bought them first, so he may sell them by right. Are the statues of your faith set up and raised? Lamps hang at the altars. You display just as many signs of your superstition. Statues, against the Word of God, Exod. 20, are erected: teachers, nurses and pillars of idolatry. Why, you sacrilegious men, do you mutilate the Decalogue and strike out the precept about idols, that they are neither to be made nor worshipped? For in the office of the Virgin Mary, which is in use among the Romanists today, printed both in Latin and in French at Paris, with the privilege of Pope Sixtus V and corrected by order of Pius V, the precepts are read: "You shall have no other gods before me," "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain." O sacrilege! The holy Fathers condemn this, who forbid idols, that is statues and images, to be cast (for even the Papists themselves regard idol and image as equivalent: Cajetan the cardinal on Exodus 20, and Durandus the bishop in Rationale, book 1, chapter 3, with Isidore, De origine, chapter 11). Clement of Alexandria, Stromata books 1 and 5; Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica book 3; Athanasius in his oration against Gregory of Sabellius; indeed all the way down to Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith book 4, chapter 17; and Bellarmine too, On Images book 2, chapter 8; Durandus on Deuteronomy 4, question 5; Pérez on traditions, part 3, in the treatise on images; and the Abulensis confess that the Fathers agree with us. Altars also pertain not to the New but to the Old Testament, if you speak properly and not figuratively, for altars look toward victims. But the ancients did speak figuratively of wooden tables as altars. Thus Athanasius complains of the Arians who burned wooden tables, in his letter to those living a solitary life. See also Optatus against Parmenian book 6, and Augustine, On the Words of the Lord according to John, sermon 46. Do you further wish to prove the truth of your religion by lamps set against the midday sun? Very prudent and very modest! The ancients used lamps, but out of necessity, not by will, a ceremony added to religion. For Pliny rightly bears witness to this in Letter 97, book 10, to Trajan: "They were accustomed to assemble on a fixed day before dawn." To the same point returns the boasting of the Jesuits, who say that we cannot deny that Christ instituted the supper by candlelight. For he instituted it on the night in which he was betrayed, 1 Cor. 11. On the earlier custom see Epiphanius, book 9, volume 2; Jerome, Against Vigilantius, chapter 7: "We do not light candles by day," he says, "as you falsely slander us. We use lights as a moderation of the darkness, that we may keep watch for the light, lest we sleep with you in darkness." Lactantius Firmianus also writes on this matter, Institutes book 6, chapter 62; although Antonius Raudensis, in his index of errors, reckons this among the errors of Lactantius, the papistical assailant of an orthodox Father and patron of the pagans, whom even Seneca, a heathen, would not unjustly laugh at if he were alive, repeating words from his book On the Happy Life, chapter 27: "When somewhere on the road a sudden cry goes up, and an old man in linen garments, with a laurel branch, holding a lamp in the middle of the day, shouts that some god is angry, you run together, you listen, you declare him divine, feeding one another's amazement." Further, the Jesuit displays sacred vestments in which images are seen woven with gold, silver and jewels. But religion admits its majesty when it admits simplicity. The splendour of vestments is new, not truly ancient. Walafrid Strabo, On Ecclesiastical Matters, chapter 24, bears witness that at first the mass (for so in that age they called the eucharist) was celebrated in ordinary dress, as is still said of some in the East. But the ridiculous garb of the priests was at length increased along with superstition. Let Tertullian be read in his book On the Pallium; and above all Pope Celestine, Letter 2 to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 1, in which he falsely mocks that superfluous vanity of vestments and teaches that teachers must be distinguished from the people by doctrine, not by tunic; by life, not by dress; by purity of understanding, not by care of the body. Leaving aside the vestments, "the chalices, the plates, the walls of the temples and the windows cry out how many and what notable men and women have poured out their life and blood for the Calvinist faith and doctrine," as the Jesuit jest has it. Our martyrs are holier to us than those whose names you...

units.la: Thrasonum more in calicibus, in patellis, in parietibus, in fenestris pingere & traducere velimus. Viget eorum memoria in coelo, ubi sub altari animæ martyrorum propter verbum Dei, & propter testimonium, quod tuebantur, clamant voce magna, dicentes: Usquequo Domine, qui sanctus es & verax, non judicas, et sanguinem nostrum vindicas, eum reposcendo abs, qui habitant in terra? Apoc. 6.10. Sic de sanctis nostris gloriari liberet, possemus verius, quam vos de Francisco vestro stigmatizato, de Dominico, de Georgio Cappadoce, homine hæretico, improbo, Arriano; qui quum ab ethnicis sub Juliano apostata crudeliter interfectus, cadaver ejus combustum est, & cineres ejus in mare projecti, ut est apud Ammianum Marcell. lib. 22. de Catharina vestra, quæ Costi regis filia dicitur, à vobis colitur; de Chriftophoro homine giganteo, contra omnem fidem ac veritatem veteris historiæ gloriamini. Verum gloria nostra Deus est. Tandem falsos ecclesiasticos producis. Quare habent illi canonem sanctorum vestrorum. Miseria nova. Potestas illa canonis ignota fuit patribus usque ad annum Christi 880, quando Adrianus sibi hoc jus usurpavit. Quod etiam Alexander tertius postea c. 1. extrav. de reliquiis sanctorum confirmavit. Interim fasti ecclesiastici notant nomina apostolorum, à quorum fide nos pendemus toti, vos defecistis omnes. Inanis ergo gloriatio est de nomine, cujus res vobis non amplius suppetit, Sed de his satis.
units.tr: You would like to paint and boast of them on the chalices, the plates, the walls and the windows, in the manner of braggarts. Their memory flourishes in heaven, where under the altar the souls of the martyrs who were slain for the word of God and for the testimony they held cry out with a loud voice, saying: "How long, Lord, holy and true, do you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" Rev. 6:10. We might rightly boast of our saints in this way, more truly than you of your stigmatized Francis, of Dominic, of George of Cappadocia, a heretic, a wicked man, an Arian, who when he was cruelly killed by the pagans under the apostate Julian, his corpse was burned and his ashes thrown into the sea, as is recorded in Ammianus Marcellinus, book 22; of your Catherine, said to be the daughter of King Costus, who is worshipped by you; of Christopher, a giant of a man, you boast against all faith and truth of ancient history. But our glory is God. Finally you produce false ecclesiastics. Hence they have a canon of your saints. A new wretchedness. That power of canonization was unknown to the Fathers until the year of Christ 880, when Hadrian usurped this right to himself. Which Alexander III afterwards also confirmed in chapter 1, Extravagantes, On the Relics of the Saints. Meanwhile the ecclesiastical calendars record the names of the apostles, on whose faith we all depend; you have all deserted them. It is an empty boast, then, to glory in a name whose reality no longer remains to you. But enough of these things.

units.la: Conclusio nona.
units.tr: Ninth Conclusion.

units.la: Verum ac sincerum Dei cultus est actus totius hominis secundum singulas ejus partes; secundum animam, eamque totam, & singulas ejus facultates, & secundum corpus, quae illud animae instrumentum, capax & ipsum, mediante anima, beatitudinis. Dico actum, qui nempe ab homine proficiscitur, omnium praestantissimus, & velut continuus, adeo ut quivis alius actus, qui ab homine patrantur per voluntatis aliquem interventum, secundum istum & normam ejus debeant praestari. Et Socolovius Jesuita quidem tradit hunc actum partim esse internum, partim externum, quorum hic consistit in rebus, personis, & circumstantiis & instrumentis. Res est in sacrificiis, Mal. 1. 10. in caerimoniis, Gen. 26. 7. In votis, Psal. 76. 12. 1. Tim. 2. 1. In hymnis, psalmis, canticis spiritualibus Eph. 5. in labore & aerumna, in vigiliis multis, in fame, in siti, in jejuniis multis, in frigore & nuditate, in sui ipsius castigatione, omniq; carnis mortificatione, referente & lanciente haec omnia Paulo 2. Cor. 11. Personae cultui divino destinatae in scriptu- ris leguntur, non pontifices novi testamenti, ut placet Jesuitæ, sed presbyteri, non sacerdo-tes, quos jactat papatus, sed diaconi, & auditores, quibus superstitio adjunxit acoluthos, lectores, ostiarios, exorcistas, monachos, eremitas, virgines Deo scilicet devotas. Circum-stantiæ & instrumenta cultus divini, quem Christiani præstant, sunt templa, sacræ mensæ, dies festi supplicationum, jejuniorum, pœnitentiæ, quibus papistæ assumunt altaria, vasorum amplam supellectilem, vestitum, quem putant sacrum &c. Quapropter externum Dei cultu juxta verbi divini decretum ecclesiæ reformatæ habent, & splendidum contra Jesuitæ mendacium ita sonat: Sacrificium visibile habent nullum, vota nulla, cerimonias nullas, sacrorum & cerimoniarum antistites nullos, templa apud eos sunt demolita, altaria eversa, sacra vasa conflata, virginitas irrisa, pro Davidicis psalmis, qui de ore ecclesiæ Judæis ipsis testibus nunquam recedere debebant, canticæ quædam aulicorum hominum introducta sunt. Ne patet quidem omnis mendacii mendacium grandius excogitare ac proferre potuisset. Sacrificia habemus visibilia. Offerimus enim nos ipsi gratas Deo victimas. Visi-biles vero sumus. Vota nobis sunt quotidiana, & preces. Id publica docet ecclesiæ nostræ & familiarum praxis. Cerimoniæ sunt pau-cæ quidem, at cultu divino dignæ, & abapostolis acceptæ. Templa non demolimur, sed verbi præconio & pietatis exercitio exornamus. Altaria non evertimus, sed in tabulas Dei convertimus, in quibus panem Domini edimus. Sacra vasa, quæ usui esse queunt ecclesiæ, asservamus. Virginitatem non irridemus, sed custodimus & laudamus: stupra autem vestra virginitatis titulo velata sive venustata exsecramur. Psalmi Davidici apud nos clarè sonant, fescenninæ [?] atq; impuræ aulicorum cantilenæ prohibentur, non canuntur, non audiuntur in ecclesiis nostris. Lustrato omnia nostra sacra, & totidem âte mendacia in nos prolata, quot verba experieris.
units.tr: True and sincere worship of God is an action of the whole man according to each of his parts: according to the soul, and that whole soul, and each of its faculties; and according to the body, which is the instrument of the soul, itself also capable, through the soul, of blessedness. I say an action, which indeed proceeds from man, most excellent of all and, as it were, continuous, so that every other action which is performed by man through some intervention of the will ought to be rendered according to this action and its norm. And Socolovius the Jesuit indeed teaches that this action is partly internal and partly external, of which the external consists in things, persons, circumstances and instruments. The things are in sacrifices (Mal. 1.10), in ceremonies (Gen. 26.7), in vows (Ps. 76.12; 1 Tim. 2.1), in hymns, psalms and spiritual songs (Eph. 5); in labour and toil, in many watchings, in hunger, in thirst, in many fastings, in cold and nakedness, in the chastising of oneself and the mortifying of every flesh, Paul relating and listing all these things (2 Cor. 11). The persons destined for divine worship are read of in the Scriptures: not the high priests of the New Testament, as the Jesuit pleases to have it, but elders, not the priests whom the papacy boasts of, but deacons and hearers, to whom superstition has added acolytes, readers, doorkeepers, exorcists, monks, hermits, and virgins devoted to God. The circumstances and instruments of the divine worship which Christians render are the temples, the holy tables, the feast days, the days of supplication, of fasting and of repentance; to these the Papists add altars, an ample furniture of vessels, the vestments which they think sacred, and so on. Therefore the Reformed churches have external worship of God according to the decree of the divine Word, and against the Jesuit's lie this splendid declaration rings out: "They have no visible sacrifice, no vows, no ceremonies, no ministers of the sacred rites and ceremonies; their temples have been demolished, their altars overthrown, their sacred vessels melted down, virginity mocked; in place of the Davidic psalms, which ought never to have departed from the mouth of the Church, the Jews themselves being witnesses, certain songs of courtly men have been introduced." Indeed, no one could have devised and produced a greater lie than this, the lie of every lie. We have visible sacrifices, for we offer ourselves as acceptable victims to God; and we are visible. We have daily vows and prayers; the public practice of our churches and of our households teaches this. Our ceremonies are few indeed, yet worthy of divine worship, and received from the apostles. We do not demolish temples, but adorn them with the proclamation of the Word and the exercise of piety. We do not overthrow altars, but turn them into tables of God, at which we eat the Lord's bread. The sacred vessels which can be of use to the Church we keep safe. We do not mock virginity, but guard and praise it; your fornications, veiled or made attractive under the name of virginity, we curse. The Davidic psalms sound clearly among us; obscene and impure songs of courtly men are forbidden, are not sung, and are not heard in our churches. Examine all our sacred things, and you will find as many lies brought against us as words.

units.la: Sed ne prævaricari potius, quàm vero patrocinari velle videamur, Socolovii corollarium, quod se in honorem beatissimæ virginis Mariæ addidisse scribit, ponderandum quoq; erit. In vera, inquit, ecclesia debet esse perennis veneratio matris Dei: hoc enim ipsa in spiritu Dei prædixit: Ecce enim ex hoc beata me dicent omnes generationes: quia fecit mihi magna qui potens est, & sanctum nomen ejus. Quum igitur in istorum synagogis mater Dei non modo non prædicetur tantum, sed blasphemetur, nonnunquam proscindatur ac producatur, graveq; nefas putetur, si angelica salutatione honoretur; profecto non erunt de illis generationibus, de quibus illa prædixit, beatam eam prædicaturas in perperennis[?]; sed ex illius principis cohorte potius, de quo dictum est: Inimicitias ponam inter te & inter mulierem, & illa calcabit super caput tuum, & tu insidiaberis calcaneo ejus: proculq;[?] ab illa domo erunt, in qua beati habitantes omnes, quia in aeternum laudabunt Dominum: remotissimi ab ecclesia sanctorum, remotissimi a populo gravi, in quo benedicitur Domin. Omnia haec sunt φορικά[?]. Quid enim? 1· Veneratio perennis matris Dei non est nota veteris ecclesiae, nisi in cerebro Socolovii nata. Antiquitas enim eam ignorat, scriptura non ita commendat.
units.tr: But lest we seem to prevaricate rather than to plead for the truth, the corollary of Socolovius, which he writes he added in honour of the most blessed Virgin Mary, must also be weighed. "In the true Church," he says, "there ought to be a perpetual veneration of the Mother of God; for she herself foretold this by the Spirit of God: 'For behold, from now on all generations shall call me blessed, because he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.'" Since, then, in the synagogues of these men the Mother of God is not only not proclaimed, but is blasphemed, sometimes torn to pieces and dragged about, and it is thought a grave crime if she is honoured with the angelic salutation, surely they will not be of those generations of which she foretold that they would call her blessed in perpetuity; rather they belong to that prince's band of whom it was said: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and she shall bruise your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel." They will be far from that house in which all who dwell are blessed, because they shall praise the Lord for ever; most remote from the Church of the saints, most remote from the holy people in whom the Lord is blessed. All these are φορικά [?]. For what? (1) The perpetual veneration of the Mother of God is unknown to the ancient Church and was born only in the brain of Socolovius. Antiquity is ignorant of it, and Scripture does not commend it in this way.

units.la: 2· Luditur ambiguitate à Jesuita. Aliud n. est venerari, i.e. honorare ut hominem omnium beatissimum: aliud vero adorare. Honoramus quidem beatam virginem supra omnes mulieres, at adorare eam ex scripturis non didicimus.
units.tr: (2) The Jesuit plays on an ambiguity. For it is one thing to venerate, that is, to honour her as the most blessed of all human beings; it is another to adore. We indeed honour the blessed Virgin above all women, but we have not learned from the Scriptures to adore her.

units.la: 3· Matrem Dei ab ecclesia nostra blasphemari, plusquam virulenta calumnia est.
units.tr: (3) That our Church blasphemes the Mother of God is more than a virulent calumny.

units.la: 4· Non grave, sed nullum nefas est eam salutatione angelica honorari, sed salutationem illam in religiosam adorationem vertere, id vero blasphemum simul ac sacrilegum censemus. Doctri enim sumus à magistro nostro unico Matth. 4. v. 10. Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & ei soli servies. Et sane non nisi eum adorare cum religione didicimus, in cujus nomen baptizati sumus. At vero in solius Dei nomen baptizati sumus. Ergo cum solúm religiose adorare decet, Cui n, una parte cultus divini competit, eidem & altera, imo totus. Si a[?], vel partem cultus divini, vel totum creaturae transscripserimus, egregio ecclesiam principio spoliabimus, quo adversus antitrinitarios & Arianos deitatem filii ac Spiritus S. asserit. Esta[?]. illud a cultu Dei, ab invocatione, a baptismo, & id genus aliis, soli Deo debitis. Bellarminus contra eos scribens, qui negarunt deitatem Sp.s., oppugnat eos ex hoc dicto: baptizate omnes gentes in nomen patris, filii & Sp.sancti: significans Dominum non conjunctum fuisse cum filio Sp. sanctum, nisi verus esset Deus. Interim tu no[?] dubitas in precibus conjungere beatam virginem cum S. trinitate[?] & socius tuus Gregorius de Valentia tractatus suos hac gratiarum actione obsignate haud gravatur: Laus Deo & virgini Mariae, item Iesu Christo filio aeterno Dei aeterni. Et Bellarminus, Laus Deo, virginiq; matri Maria, tom.1. edit. Ingolstadianae. Gregorius de Valentia in fine omnium pene tractatuum. Ita belli disputatores quod una manu porrigitis, altera eripitis! Suus ergo Deo fit honos, suus beatae virgini, qua, ut par est, amamus & honoramus, inter alias intelligentes Dei creaturas. Corollarium ergo tuum est vanissimum, Socolovi. Non tamen obticescis, sed porro obloqueris: quomodo ille religione aliqua imbutus esse putandus est, qui nullum certum modum, nullam certam rationem divinum uminis colendi habet? nullos ritus, nullas ceremonias certas amplexus est? Itaque praeclare professi illi ipsi, ad quos ista non ita pridem provocarunt, orientales patres contra illos ferunt sententiam, &c. Res ipsa te refutat, si nos perstringis dicto; verborum testimonio quid opus est? Lege ecclesiarum confessiones, & quidem harmonicas. Hæ certum ac verum cultus divini modum habet & præscribunt. Ubi est os tuum, ubi fros, nisi plane ess effrons? Patres orientales nō tā nobis adversantur, quam infestant superstitionem & ambitū Romanū. Et bene cecidit, quod 2. Chron. c.11 v. 3. allegasti. Verē n. hujus calamitosi seculi & status pictura in Israelitis illis priscis ibi cernitur, quae nunquam ab oculis, imo ab animo discedere ja debeat. Aitā Spiritus Dei: Dominus fuit vobiscum dum fuistis cum eo, & si requiritis eum, præsto erit vobis; sin derelinquetis eum, derelinquet vos. Dies enim multi aguntur Israelitis sine Deo vero, et sine sacerdote docente, ac sine lege. Quod si conversum fuisset, quum angustia esset sibi, ad Dominum Deum Israelis; requirentibus ipsum præsto fuisset illis. Sed temporibus istis non est pax exeunti & redeunti; verum vexationes magnae super omnes habitatores regionum. Adeo ut contundantur gens gente, & civitas civitate; quia Deus vexat eos omni angu-stia, stia[?]. Vos ergo confirmamini, neq; sint remissæ manus vestræ: est n. merces operi vestro. Bella enim & bellici rumores, qui passim nunc disseminantur, nos pariter omnes ad serium pietatis studium ac pœnitentiam excitare debet, ut iram Dei placemus, & antichristum tàdem fundamus, pace & justitia perpetua fruituri.
units.tr: (4) It is not a grave but no crime at all to honour her with the angelic salutation; but to turn that salutation into religious adoration, this we judge to be at once blasphemous and sacrilegious. For we are taught by our one Master: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone" (Matt. 4.10). And indeed we have learned to adore with religion only him into whose name we have been baptized. But we have been baptized into the name of God alone. Therefore, since it is fitting to adore religiously only that one, to whom one part of divine worship belongs, to the same belongs the other part too, indeed the whole. If we transfer either a part of divine worship or the whole to a creature, we shall strip the Church of an excellent principle, by which it asserts against the Antitrinitarians and Arians the deity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Let that be taken from the worship of God, from invocation, from baptism, and other such things owed to God alone. Bellarmine, writing against those who denied the deity of the Holy Spirit, attacks them from this saying: "Baptize all nations in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit," signifying that the Lord would not have joined the Holy Spirit with the Son unless he were true God. Meanwhile you do not hesitate to join the blessed Virgin with the Holy Trinity in prayers, and your companion Gregory of Valencia does not hesitate to seal his treatises with this thanksgiving: "Praise to God and to the Virgin Mary, likewise to Jesus Christ the eternal Son of the eternal God." And Bellarmine: "Praise to God and to the virgin mother Mary," vol. 1, Ingolstadt edition. Gregory of Valencia at the end of almost all his treatises. Thus you warlike disputants take away with one hand what you offer with the other! Honour is therefore given to God as his own, and to the blessed Virgin as hers, whom, as is fitting, we love and honour among the other creatures of God that understand. Your corollary therefore is most vain, Socolovius. Yet you do not fall silent, but go on objecting: "How is he to be thought imbued with any religion who has no fixed mode and no fixed rule of worshipping the divine majesty? who has embraced no rites, no certain ceremonies?" Therefore those very men whom you recently provoked with these words, the eastern Fathers, pronounce a sentence against them, etc. The thing itself refutes you, if you assail us with a saying; what need is there of a testimony of words? Read the confessions of the churches, and indeed the harmonised ones. These have and prescribe a fixed and true mode of divine worship. Where is your mouth, where your forehead, unless you are plainly shameless? The eastern Fathers are not so much opposed to us as they attack superstition and Roman ambition. And your citation of 2 Chronicles 11.3 turned out well; for in those ancient Israelites a true picture of this calamitous age and state is seen there, which ought never to depart from our eyes, indeed from our minds. Hear the Spirit of God: "The Lord was with you while you were with him; and if you seek him, he will be found by you; but if you forsake him, he will forsake you. For many days Israel was without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without the law. But if they had turned, when they were in distress, to the Lord God of Israel, and sought him, he would have been present to them. But in those times there is no peace for the one going out or the one coming in, but great troubles over all the inhabitants of the lands, so that nation is broken by nation and city by city, because God troubles them with every distress." [Then the text continues:] "But you, be strong, and let not your hands be slack, for there is a reward for your work." For wars and rumours of wars, which are now spread everywhere, ought equally to stir us all to a serious zeal for piety and to repentance, so that we may appease the wrath of God and at last overthrow Antichrist, enjoying a perpetual peace and righteousness.

units.la: Conclusio decima.
units.tr: Tenth Conclusion.

units.la: Verus & sincerus Dei cultus, omnesq; ejus partes sunt certum ecclesiæ Dei documentum. In hac cōclusione est aliquid veri, aliquid etiam falsi. Verūm est, imò verissimū, quod cultus Dei sincerus sit certum ecclesiæ Dei documentum. Id idem est, quod supra asseruimus de communicati-ōne verbi Dei, quàm unicam ecclesiæ Dei notam statuimus. Falsum, quod omnes ejus partes sint ta-le documentum. Internus Dei cultus, qui tamen pars est cultus divini, & quidē princeps, nō est nota ecclesiæ. soli n. Deo est conspicuus, hominum nemini. Hoc etiam fatetur Socolovius lib. 3. c. 6. idcoq; hactenus eum ecclesiæ notā esse nobiscū diffi-tetur. Sed externi etiā cultus quædā partes ecclesiā non certò indicant. Non sacrificia quævis. Sunt enim illa apud varias gentes, etiam à Deo alienas. Non vota omnia, sed jussu Dei facta. Non hymni quivis, sed verbi communicationem habentes. Nō personæ, non templa, non vasa, non cerimoniæ, nō tempora. Hac n. fraude diabolum jam inde ab initio tam idolorum cultores, quàm hæreticos miserè decepisse, Tertullianus vetus & gravis scriptor de præscriptionibus hæreticorum pulcerrimè demon-strat: Diabolus, inquit, cujus sunt partes invertēdi veritatem, ipsas quoq; res divinorum sacramentorum in idolorum mysteriis æmulatur. Tingit & ipse quosdam utiq; credentes & fideles suos, expiatione de lavacro repromittit, etsi adhuc meminit mythra, signat illic in fronte milites suos, celebrat & panis oblationem, & imaginem resurrectionis inducit, & sub gladio redimit corona. Quid quod & summum pontificem in ipsius nuptiis statuit? Habet quoq; virgines & cõtinetes. Hæc igitur omnia ex nota una & certissima discerni debent, ac dignosci. Manet igitur cultus Dei nota ecclesiæ, sed nõ quovis modo, sed quatenus & actum, & modum, & obligationem habet ex verbi divini tanquam ejus normæ communicatione, ex qua nascitur confessio illa fidelium, quam quisq; Christianus jure merito his afflictissimis temporibus, reiq; publicæ concussione edit cum Davide psal. 35. v. 17. 18. Domine, quamdiu auspicies? reduc animam meam à vastationibus eorum, à juvenibus leonibus unicam meam: celebrabo te in congregatione multa: in populo frequenti laudabo te.
units.tr: The true and sincere worship of God, and all its parts, are a certain evidence of the Church of God. In this conclusion there is something true and something false. It is true, indeed most true, that sincere worship of God is a certain evidence of the Church of God. This is the same as what we asserted above concerning the communication of the Word of God, which we established as the single mark of the Church of God. What is false is that all its parts are such an evidence. Internal worship of God, which is nevertheless a part of divine worship, and indeed the chief part, is not a mark of the Church. For it is visible to God alone, and to no man. Socolovius also admits this in book 3, chapter 6, and therefore up to this point he concedes with us that it is not a mark of the Church. But certain parts of external worship also do not certainly indicate the Church. Not every kind of sacrifice: for such things are found among various nations, even among those who are alien to God. Not all vows, but only those made by the command of God. Not every hymn, but those that have communion with the Word. Not persons, not temples, not vessels, not ceremonies, not times. For by this trick the devil has miserably deceived, from the very beginning, both the worshippers of idols and the heretics, as Tertullian, an ancient and weighty writer, most beautifully demonstrates in his book on the prescription of heretics: The devil, he says, whose part it is to pervert the truth, imitates in the mysteries of idols the very things of the divine sacraments. He himself also baptizes certain believers and his own faithful; he promises forgiveness of sins through the bath; if he still remembers Mithras, he marks his soldiers on the forehead there; he celebrates also the offering of bread, and introduces the image of the resurrection, and at the sword he redeems with a crown. Why, he even sets up a chief priest at his marriages? He also has virgins and the continent. All these things, therefore, must be distinguished and recognised from one mark, and the most certain one. The worship of God therefore remains a mark of the Church, but not in any manner whatever: rather insofar as it has its act, its manner and its obligation from the communication of the divine Word, as from its rule, out of which arises that confession of the faithful which every Christian rightly and deservedly utters in these most afflicted times and in the shaking of the public weal, with David, Psalm 35, verses 17 and 18: Lord, how long wilt thou look on? Rescue my soul from their devastations, my only one from the young lions. I will praise thee in the great congregation; in the crowded people I will laud thee.

units.la: Cæterùm Mülhufinus thef. 5. huc quoq; refert id, quod omnes omnium temporū hæreses fuerint inconstantes, & novam quasi ecclesiæ notā hinc [?]eudit, deniq; addit hanc prorsus intactam à nobis, conscientia scilicet de perpetua dogmatum nostrorum varietate ac inconstantia convictis, quodq; nihil reperissemus in ea, quod vel per calumniam in catholicos Romanos retorqueremus. Sed esto, fuerint omnes omnium temporū hæreses inconstantes, an ideo hinc nota ecclesiæ erit fabricanda, quæ diversa sit ab ea, quam nunc refellimus? Non attigimus hanc, non quod invictam putaremus, & nos inconstantiæ convictos, sed quod ean-dem cum præ gressa judicaremus aut nullam. Etenim qui solam religionem veram docet constante, is cæteras omnes dicit inconstantes. Supervacuum ergo fuit de hæreseon inconstantia hic commentari. Quæ vero Calvino exprobras, ea ex Bellarmino expilasti, ubi diluta sunt. Nōdū vero ulla vidim[?] doctrinæ, in qua salutis viam habemus, inconstantiam jure objectam esse. Ideo salva adhuc conscientia eam ut veram, ut orthodoxam, ut constanter retinemus. Trinitarii, quos vocas, sed rectius Tritheitæ, in Transylvania, & Libertini in Gallia non magis nocet doctrinæ nostræ, quæ adversus eos hactenus viget, quam vestram depascunt. Ab his nihil metuimus nobis, nihil ecclesiæ nostræ; sed vos & eos ad veritatem cum pietate consociatam perducere pro virili fumus annixi. Deserite ergo maledictum pontificem vestrum, & Jesu Christo in secula benedicto accedite. Si prophetas audire detrectatis, audite poetam, qui pontifices vestros, & qui eis haesuri sunt, infelicissimos ita praedicat, adeoque omnes pios ab eorum societate abster-ret:
units.tr: Moreover, Mülhufinus, in thesis 5, also brings in here the fact that all the heresies of all times have been inconstant, and from this he forges, as it were, a new mark of the Church; finally he adds that this mark is wholly untouched by us, since we are, as it were, convicted in our conscience of the perpetual variety and inconstancy of our doctrines, and that we have found nothing in it which we could even by calumny turn back upon the Roman Catholics. But granted that all the heresies of all times have been inconstant, will a mark of the Church therefore be fashioned from this, one that differs from the one we are now refuting? We have not touched upon this, not because we think it unconquered, or because we are convicted of inconstancy, but because we judged it either the same as the preceding one or none at all. For he who teaches that only his own religion is true, and constant, says that all others are inconstant. It was therefore superfluous to comment here on the inconstancy of heresies. But what you reproach Calvin with, you have plundered from Bellarmine, where it has already been refuted. Nor have we yet seen that inconstancy has been rightly objected to any doctrine in which we have the way of salvation. Therefore, with conscience still intact, we hold it as true, as orthodox, and as constant. The Trinitarians, as you call them, but more rightly Tritheists, in Transylvania, and the Libertines in France, do no more harm to our doctrine, which has so far flourished against them, than they devour your own. We fear nothing from them for ourselves, nothing for our Church; but we have striven, as far as we are able, to lead both you and them to the truth joined with piety. Abandon therefore your accursed pontiff, and come to Jesus Christ, blessed for ever. If you refuse to hear the prophets, hear the poet, who so proclaims your pontiffs, and those who will cling to them, most unhappy, and so thoroughly keeps all the pious away from their fellowship:

units.la: Flumen apud superos nullum est, quid pontibus ergo Est opus? aut quid opus deniq; pontifice? At apud infernos sunt flumina plurima. Quare Illi habeant pontes pontifices q; suos.
units.tr: There is no river among the upper gods; why then is there need of bridges, or indeed of a pontiff? But among the infernal regions there are very many rivers. Let those therefore have their bridges and their pontiffs.

units.la: Inconstantiam colligis ex Puritanorum, aliorum{§} Calvinianorum concertationibus. Sed malè. Melius vero Jac. Middendorpius theologus & JC. Colon. l. 5. Academiarum judicat: Habet, inquit, quodlibet seculi certas in doctrina offensiones, quæ efficiunt, ut theologia semper novarum disputationum varietate nō modo amplificetur, sed & quasi novam formā suscipiat. Quod quum apud Clementem Alexandrinum, Origenem, Augustinum, Damascenum, Lombardum videre sit: quid mirum hanc ætatem, tot erroribus fœcundam, novas semper doctrinæ capita excutienda non tantum offerre, sed & ingerere? Religio ergo integra manet & una, licet diversis illa seculis plenius ac planius à doctoribus data occasione explicetur.
units.tr: You gather inconstancy from the disputes of the Puritans and of other Calvinists. But badly. Better, however, does Jacob Middendorp, theologian and professor at the Academies of Cologne, judge, in book 5: "Every age has certain offences in doctrine, which cause theology to be enlarged not only by the variety of new disputations, but also to take on, as it were, a new form." Since this may be seen in Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Augustine, Damascene and Lombard, what wonder is it that this age, so fruitful in so many errors, not only offers but even thrusts upon us the need to examine new heads of doctrine? Religion therefore remains whole and one, although in different ages it has been explained more fully and plainly by the teachers, as occasion was given.

Τὴν γὰρ ἀναβάλλει ὅσον αἰεὶ ὁ αὐτὸς ὁλυμπ[?]ῳ· Καὶ τὰν ἀχρήστων ὡς κρεῖττον[?] Οὕτως δυσέβιν νικᾷ τὰ χαλεπὰ πάντα, Καὶ χάρις ἱμεροεσσα ἀεὶ σὺν ἀδ[illegible, ~6 letters] Τῇ παιδὸς, ὅστις ἐὼ ὧν τῷ βίῳ ἐννομία ῥέζει. units.tr: The Greek verses are a dedicatory poem of which the Latin transcription is too corrupt to restore with confidence. Its legible sense: the author praises the one who casts off the empty talk of men and shows the gifts of wisdom (Jesus) and of our calling; he speaks of Abraham as one who endures all hardships through faith, and of the Spirit's power by which the Church, chosen and kept by God, is sustained. [Greek verses partly illegible; the translation above is a summary of their drift, not a line-by-line rendering.]

units.la: Laus magna est patriam defendere fortibus armis, Sed maior sanctam Christi defendere sponsam. Ergo tibi merito laudes, Abraham, sonare Gestio, quod gladio Jovæ, gladioque GIDHONIS (Nempe Dei verbo) sanctum defendis ovile; Dum sub vexillo CHRISTI committere pugnam Audes. Præclara hæc certamina perge subire, Perge fidem servare Deo, cursumq; salutis Sic age. Sic debitur tandem tibi pulcra corona, Quam meruit CHRISTUS, nec non tibi reddet in ævum.
units.tr: Great is the praise of defending one's country with brave arms, but greater is the praise of defending the holy spouse of Christ. Therefore, Abraham, I rejoice to sound your praises deservedly, because you defend the holy fold with the sword of Jehovah and the sword of Gideon (that is, with the Word of God); while under the banner of Christ you dare to join battle. Go on to undertake these splendid conflicts, go on to keep the faith toward God and the course of salvation: so act. So at last a fair crown is owed to you, which Christ has earned, and it will also be rendered to you for ever.
